sections.title: Kinematics and Statics of Tendon Actuation
Analysis and control of tendon-driven fingers

scenes.title: Forbidden Directions
scenes.brief: A 2D/3D configuration space drawn as a slate floor. At the current state q a lime fan shows the allowed velocity directions (null space of A(q)) and coral arrows show the forbidden ones (rows of A). Toy 1: two blue beads joined by a slate rod; drag one bead and the other follows, a purple tension arrow along the rod. Toy 2: a shopping-cart / skate whose blade forbids sideways motion; the coral arrow rotates with the heading. A toggle "integrable?" either draws the gold level-surface h(q)=0 the system is trapped on, or shows the cart wandering anywhere though its velocity is always in the lime fan. A work meter (Γ·q̇) stays pinned at 0 for every constraint force.

scenes.title: Constraint Forces
scenes.brief: A blue bead in the xy-plane under gravity, simulated in the full unconstrained coordinates q=(x,y). Turn on the constraint and a purple arrow Aᵀλ appears exactly along the constraint normal, sized live by λ = (AM⁻¹Aᵀ)⁻¹(AM⁻¹(F−Cq̇−N)+Ȧq̇). The bead then traces a circle (pendulum) instead of falling. A tension gauge reads λ; it swells at the bottom of the swing (speed² term) and with mass. Drag the bead to change the swing height; a bar chart shows the two parts of the tension (gravity part and spin part).

scenes.title: Project & Drop
scenes.brief: At a configuration q, a lime plane (null space of A) and a coral normal. Arbitrary blue "Newton residual" arrow (d/dt ∂L/∂q̇ − ∂L/∂q − Υ) is dropped onto the lime plane: its shadow must vanish, the coral part is soaked up by purple constraint forces. Then the coordinates split into free orange knobs q₁ and slaved blue q₂ = −A₂⁻¹A₁q₁. Main toy: a coin rolling on a slate floor with orange steering and driving torque sliders; the reduced 2×2 dynamics in (θ,φ) run, and a pink trail (x,y) is drawn by integrating ẋ=ρcosθφ̇, ẏ=ρsinθφ̇.

scenes.title: Substitution Trap
scenes.brief: Two simulated twins of the same skate-like system run side by side from the same start: lime twin uses "unconstrained L → Lagrange-d'Alembert → apply constraint"; coral twin plugs the constraint into L first. Their pink trails diverge; a coral gap meter grows. The extra force on the coral twin is drawn as a ghost coral arrow equal to the right-hand side of Eq (6.15). Toggle the constraint to a gradient one (a = ∇h): the ghost arrow shrinks to zero because the two crossed partial-derivative tiles ∂²h/∂rᵢ∂rⱼ and ∂²h/∂rⱼ∂rᵢ snap onto each other and cancel.

scenes.title: Hand as Arm
scenes.brief: Two orange-jointed planar fingers and a blue box, first floating apart, each with its own inertia ellipse. Snap the grasp: teal contact dots lock, and the finger inertias are pulled through J_h⁻¹Gᵀ and added onto the box, so the box's blue inertia ellipse visibly grows into M̃ = M_o + GJ_h⁻ᵀM_fJ_h⁻¹Gᵀ. Drag the gold target pose; joint torques τ map to a pink object wrench F = GJ_h⁻ᵀτ. A skew meter (xᵀ(dM̃/dt−2C̃)x) stays at 0 while the grasp moves.

scenes.title: Hidden Squeeze
scenes.brief: Two fingertips hold a blue box. Purple arrows at the teal contacts show λ (the Lagrange multipliers). A slider adds a pure internal squeeze (a null-space-of-G force): the purple arrows grow toward each other but the box's net-wrench arrow stays at zero. Then swing the grasp fast: even with torques that carry no squeeze, the purple arrows change because of the dynamic terms Mθ̈+Cθ̇+N; a split bar shows "commanded" vs "dynamic" internal force. Freeze motion and the dynamic slice disappears.

scenes.title: Teamwork Robots
scenes.brief: Same J θ̇ = Gᵀẋ template, three skins. (1) Two/three orange-jointed arms rigidly grip one blue beam (teal welded contacts, G built from adjoints); lifting it shows the combined effective inertia ellipse. (2) One arm holding a pink welding tip: drag the gold target in workspace; the effective inertia ellipse M̃ = M_o + J⁻ᵀM_fJ⁻¹ drawn at the tip balloons toward infinity as the arm nears a singularity, while a joint-space inertia readout stays finite. (3) Chalk on a slate board: a lime motion direction along the board and a purple push into the board; the push slider changes contact force but not the motion.

scenes.title: Spare Joints
beats: ➕ too many or too few joints
scenes.brief: A 3-link planar arm (orange joints, pink tip) with the tip pinned to a gold dot. The null-space self-motion slider v_N swings the elbows while the tip stays fixed (lime trail of the elbows, pink tip motionless). J is drawn as two rows, K as a third row stacked under it to make a square J̄; a determinant meter shows J̄ invertible except when all links align (🚫 flash). Toggle K choices: K=[0 0 1] (a real angle) vs the orthogonal K; for the latter, walk a small loop of v_N and ẋ and the arm returns with the tip home but θ shifted, proving v_N is not the rate of any coordinate. Dynamics view: inertia ellipse in (x, y, v_N) space from J̄⁻ᵀMJ̄⁻¹.

scenes.title: Stuck Directions
scenes.brief: A blue object held by fingers whose J_h lacks rank. Around the object, a 3D velocity ball: lime directions are those the fingertips can track (W = span of H), coral directions are not. Drag the object along a coral direction and it refuses: a purple structural force appears inside the hand resisting it. Drag along lime and it moves, fingers following with θ̇ = J_h⁺ḠᵀW. The effective inertia ellipse is drawn only inside the lime subspace (l-dimensional) from M̃ = M_o + ḠJ_h⁺ᵀM_fJ_h⁺Ḡᵀ.

scenes.title: SCARA Pinch
beats: 🦾 two SCARA fingers hold a box
🔄 spin about the contact line forbidden
✂️ cut the bad spin with H
scenes.brief: Two 4-joint SCARA fingers (orange joints, pink tips) on slate bases pinch a blue box at two teal soft-finger contacts. A gold dashed line joins the contacts. Try to roll the box about that line: a coral 🚫 because the soft contacts forbid it and SCARA tips cannot tilt. Slide each finger's first three joints while the tip stays put (lime elbow trails) and an orange y-dial (sum of the three angles) records it. Then H removes the forbidden spin: the 8-entry velocity panel shrinks to 7 lime entries (w′, y), with J̄_h shown as an 8×8 tile turning into a wide-but-full-rank tile and a pseudo-inverse badge.

scenes.title: Tendon Pulleys
scenes.brief: A planar 2-joint finger (orange joints) with tendons drawn as colored strings wrapped over pulleys of radius R. Each string ends at a motor puck that you can pull with an orange force slider f_i. Moving joints changes each string's extension e_i = h_i(θ) — shown as a length bar that grows/shrinks (lime/coral). The coupling matrix P = (∂h/∂θ)ᵀ is a small grid whose entries light up when a string wraps a joint. Energy meter: f·ė equals τ·θ̇ at all times, so τ = P f. Pulling a string that goes to the outer joint also twists the inner joint (cross-coupling arrows).

scenes.title: Springy Tendons
scenes.brief: The tendon finger again, but each string has a slate spring (zig-zag) at its base, and each motor is an orange position dial e_i (stepper). The string force f_i = k_i(e_i + h_i(0) − h_i(θ)) is drawn as a purple bar on the spring. Turning a dial tightens a spring, which produces joint torques through Q = PK. With dials frozen, pushing the finger away from rest makes the springs push it back: a restoring torque arrow S(θ) plus a stiffness ellipse in joint space whose shape is PKPᵀ. A spring-stiffness slider shows a stiff tendon behaving like an inelastic one.

scenes.title: Always Taut
scenes.brief: Joint-torque plane (2 joints → 2D). Each tendon column of P is an orange arrow from the origin; since tensions are positive, reachable torques are the positive cone of those arrows (lime fill). With too few/badly placed tendons the cone misses a gold target torque (coral). Add tendons until the cone covers the whole plane: that is force-closure, equivalently P onto plus a strictly positive f_N with Pf_N = 0 (a closed loop of arrows summing to zero, drawn head-to-tail). Toggle "N+1" (one common string plus n opposers) vs "2N" (antagonist pairs). For a gold torque, the solver shows f = P⁺τ (some coral negative bars) plus the smallest preload f_N that lifts every tension bar above zero (all lime).

scenes.title: Track & Squeeze
scenes.brief: Two planar fingers (orange joints) hold a blue box; a gold trajectory for the box. Top dial: tracking gains (K_p, K_v) driving a computed-torque law on the effective dynamics M̃, C̃, Ñ; a coral error trace shrinks to zero exponentially. Second dial: desired squeeze f_N,d (purple). The torque panel shows τ split into a pink tracking part JᵀG⁺F and a purple squeeze part Jᵀf_N; changing the squeeze never changes the box path. Contact force arrows sit in teal friction cones; fast motions add a blue dynamic part that can push an arrow out (coral alarm) unless squeeze is raised. A side panel compares a pure proportional force loop (algebraic loop, no solution, flashing coral) with feedforward + integral (converges, lime).

scenes.title: Robot Lego
beats: 🧠 too big to compute at once
scenes.brief: Lego-like blocks, each a "robot" with a blue (M, C, N) badge, two input ports (gold x_d, orange F_d) and two output ports (teal x, F). Snap two finger blocks onto a payload block with an "attach" clip: the new block's badge is computed as M_p + GJ⁻ᵀM_fJ⁻¹Gᵀ. Snap a controller cap onto any block: PD caps at the bottom (fast clock icon), a feedforward cap in the middle, a computed-torque cap on top (slow clock icon); a cap that fully compensates turns its badge grey (higher levels see no dynamics). Press ▶: data pulses flow up (state queries: joints → fingertips → box) and down (forces: box → fingertips → joints). A parallel column shows the human finger hierarchy (spinal reflex loops fast, cortex slow) lining up block for block.

scenes.title: Chapter Six Map
scenes.brief: A subway map of the chapter: stations are the scene thumbnails (Forbidden Directions → Constraint Forces → Project & Drop → Substitution Trap → Hand as Arm → Hidden Squeeze → Teamwork Robots → Spare Joints / Stuck Directions / SCARA Pinch → Tendon lines → Track & Squeeze → Robot Lego). Each station shows its one key equation token colored as in its scene. Tapping a station replays a 3-second loop of that scene.

pages.summary: Chapter opener: dynamics and control of several robots sharing a task, handled by adding velocity constraints to Lagrange's equations instead of hunting for minimal coordinates.

atoms.idea: Chapter 6 title: dynamics and control of robot hands.
The chapter treats a team of robots doing one job (main case: fingers holding an object) as a single mechanical system with velocity constraints, extending the single-arm dynamics of Chapter 4.
atoms.feynman: Several kids carrying one table: each kid has their own legs, but the table forces them to move together.
atoms.visual: Opening shot: three orange-jointed fingers around a blue box; tap ▶ and the box moves along a gold path while the fingers follow, teal contact dots never sliding. A lime link icon between each fingertip and the box glows to mark the shared constraint.

atoms.idea: Section 6.1 heading: Lagrange equations with constraints.
For an open chain the usual route is: pick independent generalized coordinates that minimally cover the configuration space, then write Lagrange's equations with matching generalized forces.
atoms.feynman: A train on a track needs one number (how far along the track) to say where it is; you write its motion in that one number.
atoms.visual: A 2-link arm whose two orange joint sliders are the only coordinates; a lime checkmark shows that every slider setting is a legal pose and no extra rule is needed.

atoms.idea: For a hand, finger joint angles and object pose are coupled only through their velocities (the grasp constraint), so a clean set of independent coordinates may be hard or impossible to find.
atoms.feynman: A ball rolled between your palms: where the ball ends up depends on how you rolled it, not just on where your hands are, so you can't describe it by hand positions alone.
atoms.visual: Finger joint knobs (orange) and the box pose (blue) are drawn as separate sliders; moving a finger slider drags the box via a lime link but only through velocities — a coral ✖ appears when you try to write box pose as a function of joints.

atoms.idea: Strategy: keep all the natural (redundant) coordinates and put the constraints into the equations of motion directly, rather than eliminating them by clever coordinates; a sketch follows, with fuller treatments cited.
atoms.feynman: Instead of re-drawing the map so the road is the only place you can be, you keep the whole map and add a fence that pushes you back onto the road.
atoms.visual: Split screen: left, a bead on a wire described by one arc-length slider; right, the same bead in full (x,y) with a purple fence force keeping it on the wire. Both beads move identically.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Holonomic constraints restrict the configuration to a surface h(q)=0 with full-rank gradient; a rigid rod between two particles is the model case and its tension is the constraint force.

atoms.idea: References continue; configuration space is taken as an open subset of Rⁿ with coordinates q, using local charts for anything more general.
atoms.feynman: We pretend the world is a flat sheet of graph paper; a curved world is fine as long as you only look at a small patch at a time.
atoms.visual: A slate grid labelled with q₁,q₂ axes (red/green); a curved surface fades in and a small square patch of it flattens into the grid.

atoms.idea: Subsection 6.1.1 heading: Pfaffian constraints.

atoms.label: Eq (6.1)
atoms.idea: A constraint shrinks the set of possible paths. Example: two particles p₁,p₂ ∈ R³ tied by a massless rigid rod must keep |p₁−p₂|² = L².
atoms.feynman: Two kids holding a stick between them: whatever they do, they stay exactly one stick-length apart.
atoms.visual: Two blue beads with a slate rod; drag one bead anywhere and the other follows on a sphere of radius L (drawn as a faint lime shell). Readout |p₁−p₂| stays frozen at L.

atoms.idea: Constraints act by constraint forces that alter the motion so the rule always holds; for the rod this is the rod's tension carrying force from one particle to the other.
atoms.feynman: When one kid yanks the stick, the stick pulls the other kid along: the stick's pull is the rule enforcing itself.
atoms.visual: Pull one bead with an orange drag arrow; a purple tension arrow appears along the rod on both beads, equal and opposite, sized by how hard you pull.

atoms.label: Eq (6.2)
atoms.idea: Holonomic constraint: confines motion to a smooth hypersurface of Q, locally hᵢ(q)=0 for i=1..k, with the k×n Jacobian ∂h/∂q of full row rank (independent constraints).
atoms.feynman: A bead threaded on a bent wire: the wire is a surface you can never leave, and the rule is written just in terms of where you are.
atoms.visual: In a 3D slate configuration space, a gold surface h(q)=0; a blue bead slides only on it. The k gradient rows of ∂h/∂q are drawn as coral normals; a rank meter shows k independent arrows (flashes 🚫 if two become parallel).

atoms.idea: Terminology aside: classical names for fixed vs time-varying configuration constraints exist, but only "holonomic" is used here.
atoms.feynman: Grown-ups have three fancy words for "a fence that stays put" and "a fence that moves"; we only need one word.
atoms.visual: The gold surface first sits still, then a toggle makes it slowly drift/breathe in time; the scene only uses the still version (toggle locked to still in this beat).

atoms.idea: Because a holonomic constraint defines a smooth surface, you can pick coordinates on that surface and so eliminate the constraint.
atoms.feynman: If you live on a globe you can use latitude and longitude and forget that you're stuck on a ball.
atoms.visual: The gold constraint surface gets a lime coordinate grid painted on it; two orange sliders now move the bead freely along the grid with no constraint needed.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Holonomic constraint forces are (∂h/∂q)ᵀλ and do no work; grasping instead gives velocity-level (Pfaffian) constraints A(q)q̇=0, with A=[J_h, −Gᵀ] for a hand.

atoms.idea: Surface coordinates cover every allowed motion with no further constraint; describing a rigid body by one frame instead of its many constrained points is exactly this trick.
atoms.feynman: Instead of tracking every grain in a brick, you just say where the brick is and which way it faces.
atoms.visual: A cloud of teal points in a blue brick, each with a tiny rigid spring; collapse them into one pink frame (red/green/blue axes) that carries all points.

atoms.idea: Holonomic constraint forces are combinations of the constraint gradients: Γ = (∂h/∂q)ᵀ λ, with λ ∈ Rᵏ the force magnitudes.
atoms.feynman: A wall can only push straight out of itself; how hard it pushes is the only thing left to decide.
atoms.visual: On the gold surface the coral normal(s) at the bead; purple constraint force arrows lie exactly along them, with a λ slider showing only length changes, never direction.

atoms.idea: Constraint forces are normal to the surface and their magnitude keeps the system on it; along any feasible path their power is Γ·q̇ = λᵀ d/dt h(q) = 0.
atoms.feynman: Sliding a book along a table: the table holds the book up but doesn't speed it up or slow it down along the table.
atoms.visual: Bead slides on the gold surface; purple Γ ⟂ blue velocity arrow q̇; a power meter Γ·q̇ stays exactly 0 while a kinetic-energy bar is unaffected by the purple force.

atoms.idea: Grasping gives a genuinely different constraint, one on velocities: J_h θ̇ = Gᵀ V_po^b (finger tip velocities must match the object at the contacts).
atoms.feynman: Your hand pushing a shopping cart: wherever the cart goes, your hand's speed must match the handle's speed.
atoms.visual: Finger joints (orange) spin; the fingertip velocity arrow (pink) and the object's contact-point velocity arrow (blue) are drawn at each teal contact; they always overlap, a lime ✓ lights while equal.

atoms.idea: Pfaffian constraint: A(q)q̇ = 0 with A(q) ∈ R^{k×n} full row rank everywhere. For a hand q = (θ,x) and A = [J_h, −Gᵀ] with x local object coordinates.
atoms.feynman: A shopping cart's wheels can roll forward but not slide sideways: the rule says which way you may go right now, not where you may be.
atoms.visual: Cart icon on a slate floor; at its center a lime double-arrow (allowed) and a coral bar (forbidden sideways row of A). Rotate the cart and both rotate with it. For the hand version, A is drawn as a block bar [orange J_h | blue −Gᵀ].

atoms.idea: A Pfaffian constraint limits velocities but not necessarily positions, so it need not be expressible as an algebraic constraint on configurations; integrability is defined next.
atoms.feynman: A cart can't slide sideways, but by wiggling forward and back you can still park it anywhere.
atoms.visual: Cart starts at a gold spot; the learner drives only along lime directions; the reachable region fills the whole floor with a blue wash, showing no position is forbidden.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Integrable Pfaffian constraints equal holonomic ones; non-integrable ones are nonholonomic. Constraint forces are Aᵀλ in either case; d'Alembert's principle assumes they do no work, which holds for rolling but not sliding.

atoms.idea: Integrable: there is h:Q→Rᵏ with A(q)q̇=0 ⇔ (∂h/∂q)q̇=0. Then it is holonomic. A need not equal ∂h/∂q; they only have to allow the same velocity subspace at each q.
atoms.feynman: A rule "always move along the contour line" is secretly "stay at this height": the speed rule hides a place rule.
atoms.visual: Lime allowed-velocity arrows on a field; toggle "find h": gold level curves of h fade in and every lime arrow lies tangent to them. Rescale A's rows (coral arrows grow/shrink) and the level curves don't change.

atoms.idea: Non-integrable Pfaffian = nonholonomic: velocities lie in an (n−k)-dim subspace, but reachable configurations are not confined to an (n−k)-dim surface; such cases exist, so dynamics must handle them.
atoms.feynman: Parallel parking: you can only roll forward/back and turn, yet you can end up shifted sideways into the spot.
atoms.visual: A parallel-parking cart: lime arrows only forward/back and turning; the "Lie bracket" wiggle (forward-turn-back-turn) leaves a gold sideways gap. A counter shows dimension of reachable set (3) > allowed velocity dims (2).

atoms.idea: Even for nonholonomic constraints the constraint forces are well-defined: Γ = Aᵀ(q)λ, pushing along the rows of A; if integrable, Aᵀ and (∂h/∂q)ᵀ have the same range, matching the holonomic case.
atoms.feynman: The cart's side-friction pushes only sideways on the wheels, whether or not the cart can eventually get anywhere.
atoms.visual: The cart again: a purple side-force arrow sits on the coral forbidden row; its length λ changes as the learner turns while moving fast (bigger turn → bigger purple push).

atoms.idea: To use constraint forces in dynamics we assume they do no work and conserve energy — d'Alembert's principle.
atoms.feynman: Ice-skate blade: it stops you sliding sideways but never tires you out or gives you energy.
atoms.visual: Skate gliding on a slate rink; an energy bar (gold) stays perfectly flat while the purple side force flicks on and off during turns.

atoms.idea: Workless is reasonable for pure rolling (tiny friction losses) but fails when sliding mixes in, since then work depends on normal force; such friction is added later as an external force.
atoms.feynman: A wheel rolling doesn't wear out, but a wheel that skids burns rubber — that skid steals energy.
atoms.visual: Toggle between a rolling coin (energy bar flat) and a skidding coin (coral sparks at contact, energy bar drains). In skid mode a separate coral "friction" arrow is added after the fact.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Equations of motion with Pfaffian constraints: add Aᵀλ to Lagrange's equations; for L = ½q̇ᵀMq̇ − V, differentiating the constraint lets you solve linearly for λ.

atoms.idea: Subsection 6.1.2 heading: Lagrange multipliers.

atoms.label: Eq (6.3)
atoms.idea: Setup: configuration q ∈ Rⁿ, unconstrained Lagrangian L(q,q̇), constraints A(q)q̇=0 with A ∈ R^{k×n}, assumed smooth, independent and workless.
atoms.feynman: First imagine the bead is totally free, then remember there's a wire it has to stay on.
atoms.visual: Blue bead under gravity; a dashed slate circle (the wire) toggles on; the k=1 coral normal row A appears at the bead.

atoms.label: Eq (6.4)
atoms.idea: Treat constraint forces as one more force: d/dt ∂L/∂q̇ − ∂L/∂q + Aᵀλ − Υ = 0, with Aᵀ's columns spanning constraint-force directions and Υ the applied/nonconservative forces.
atoms.feynman: The bead's motion is gravity plus the wire's push, just as a ball on a slide is gravity plus the slide pushing back.
atoms.visual: Force diagram on the bead: slate gravity arrow, orange applied force Υ, purple Aᵀλ along the coral normal; their sum (blue) equals mass×acceleration.

atoms.idea: The k multipliers λᵢ, together with q, are found by solving (6.3) and (6.4) jointly so the constraint holds forever; each λᵢ depends on q, q̇ and the applied forces.
atoms.feynman: The wire pushes just as hard as needed — more when the bead is fast or heavy, less when it's slow.
atoms.visual: Slider for bead speed and for applied force; the purple arrow's length (λ) updates live, and a graph traces λ(t) as the bead moves.

atoms.label: Eq (6.5)
atoms.idea: With L = ½q̇ᵀM(q)q̇ − V(q): M q̈ + C q̇ + N + Aᵀλ = F. Differentiating the constraint gives A q̈ + Ȧ q̇ = 0.
atoms.feynman: If you must stay on the wire, you must also keep your speed and your speeding-up along the wire.
atoms.visual: Three stacked meters: position-on-wire error, velocity-off-wire, acceleration-off-wire — all pinned at 0. The equation tokens are colored: M blue, Aᵀλ purple, F orange.

atoms.idea: Eliminating q̈ gives a linear system (AM⁻¹Aᵀ)λ = AM⁻¹(F − Cq̇ − N) + Ȧq̇; AM⁻¹Aᵀ is invertible when the constraints are independent.
atoms.feynman: How hard the wire pushes is like asking "how much must I push back so the bead doesn't leave": one simple balance.
atoms.visual: Two-stage animation: free acceleration M⁻¹(F−Cq̇−N) drawn as a blue arrow leaving the wire; the purple correction M⁻¹Aᵀλ snaps it back tangent to the wire; the k×k matrix AM⁻¹Aᵀ shows as a small blue square that is never zero.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Explicit multiplier formula (6.6), then Example 6.1: a point-mass pendulum written in (x,y) with the length constraint x²+y²=l² as a Pfaffian constraint.

atoms.label: Fig 6.1
atoms.idea: Idealized planar pendulum: point mass m on a massless arm at angle θ, gravity down.
atoms.feynman: A ball on a string swinging from your finger.
atoms.visual: Slate pivot, slate arm, blue bob, slate gravity arrow mg; drag the bob to set the start angle.

atoms.label: Eq (6.6)
atoms.idea: λ = (AM⁻¹Aᵀ)⁻¹[AM⁻¹(F − Cq̇ − N) + Ȧq̇]; plug back into (6.5) to get the motion; λ depends only on state and applied force.
atoms.feynman: Once you know where the bead is, how fast it moves and what you're pushing, the wire's push is fully decided.
atoms.visual: A live formula panel: each factor glows when the matching arrow on the bead changes; the purple arrow length updates every frame from this formula.

atoms.label: Ex 6.1
atoms.idea: Example: treat the bob as a free 2-DOF particle and let the arm be a constraint leaving one DOF, instead of using θ.
atoms.feynman: Rather than saying "the angle of the swing", say "where the ball is in the room", and let the string keep it honest.
atoms.visual: Toggle between a one-slider θ description and the free (x,y) description with a purple string force; both bobs swing identically.

atoms.idea: q=(x,y); length constraint x²+y²=l², differentiated (and halved): [x y]·(ẋ,ẏ)=0, i.e. A(q)=[x y].
atoms.feynman: Moving along the circle means you're never moving toward or away from the center.
atoms.visual: Bob on the circle: coral radial arrow (row A = position vector), lime tangent arrow; dot product readout x·ẋ+y·ẏ = 0.

atoms.idea: Unconstrained Lagrangian ½m(ẋ²+ẏ²) − mgy; Lagrange equations become m ẍ + xλ = 0, m ÿ + mg + yλ = 0.
atoms.feynman: Each direction is just "mass times speeding-up = gravity + string pull".
atoms.visual: Two bars for x and y equations; purple string force components xλ, yλ, slate mg; bars balance at zero.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: The pendulum's multiplier is λ = −(m/l²)(gy + ẋ² + ẏ²), giving two coupled 2nd-order equations and the rod tension; then the Lagrange–d'Alembert idea: virtual displacements and virtual work.

atoms.idea: Using (6.6): λ = −(m/l²)(g y + ẋ² + ẏ²), so the equations of motion read M q̈ + (0, mg) − (1/l²)(x,y)(mgy + m(ẋ²+ẏ²)) = 0.
atoms.feynman: The string pulls harder when the ball swings fast through the bottom — like a yo-yo spun fast tugging your finger.
atoms.visual: Live tension gauge (purple) on the string; split into a slate "gravity part" and an orange "spin part" ∝ speed²; at the bottom of the swing both peak.

atoms.idea: Trade-off: two coupled 2nd-order ODEs for a 1-DOF system (more variables), but you get the rod tension explicitly: (mg/l)y + (m/l)(ẋ²+ẏ²) in magnitude.
atoms.feynman: Describing the swing with two numbers is clumsier, but now you can also read how hard the string pulls — a free bonus scale.
atoms.visual: Variable counter (2 vs 1) next to a bonus purple tension readout; crank the swing amplitude and watch tension exceed mg at the bottom; a "snap" threshold bar flashes coral if tension passes a limit.

atoms.idea: Subsection 6.1.3 heading: Lagrange–d'Alembert formulation.
Alternative: derive dynamics without computing constraint forces by projecting the motion onto feasible directions and discarding the constrained ones; this yields a compact form good for control.
atoms.feynman: If a train is on rails, you only care about pushes along the rails; the sideways pushes from the rails don't change how it speeds up.
atoms.visual: A blue force arrow on a train; its shadow on the lime rail direction (projected) is kept, the coral sideways part fades out.

atoms.idea: Allowed instantaneous directions = null space of A(q). A virtual displacement δq satisfies A(q)δq=0; virtual work δW = F·δq. d'Alembert: constraint forces do no virtual work, (Aᵀλ)·δq = 0 whenever Aδq = 0.
atoms.feynman: Imagine nudging the cart a hair in any way its wheels allow: the side-friction does zero work on every such nudge.
atoms.visual: Ghost copies of the system nudged along many lime δq directions in the null space; purple Aᵀλ arrow; a work readout (Aᵀλ)·δq stays 0 for every ghost; nudging in a coral direction is blocked.

atoms.idea: δq ≠ q̇: the actual velocity obeys both constraints and dynamics; virtual displacements obey only the constraints, and constraint forces are workless along all of them.
atoms.feynman: The path you actually walk is one of many paths the fence allows; the fence doesn't push you along any of them.
atoms.visual: Pink actual velocity arrow q̇ highlighted among a fan of lime ghost δq arrows in the null space; all lie in the lime plane, only one is real.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Projecting (6.4) on the constraint null space gives the Lagrange–d'Alembert equations (6.7)–(6.8); splitting q=(q₁,q₂) with A₂ invertible gives explicit reduced equations (6.9). Example 6.2 starts: a rolling disk.

atoms.label: Eq (6.7)–(6.8)
atoms.idea: Since (Aᵀλ)·δq = 0, the constraint force disappears: (d/dt ∂L/∂q̇ − ∂L/∂q − Υ)·δq = 0 for all δq with A(q)δq = 0. Without constraints δq is free and this is ordinary Lagrange.
atoms.feynman: Check Newton's law only along the rails; sideways it's balanced by the rails anyway.
atoms.visual: Blue residual vector r = d/dt ∂L/∂q̇ − ∂L/∂q − Υ; it must lie entirely along the coral normal: its shadow on the lime plane is drawn and pinned at zero length. Remove the constraint and the lime plane becomes all of space, forcing r = 0.

atoms.idea: Locally reorder so A = [A₁ A₂] with A₂ (k×k) invertible; with q = (q₁,q₂), Aδq=0 ⇔ δq₂ = −A₂⁻¹A₁δq₁ and δq₁ is free.
atoms.feynman: Pick some knobs you may turn freely; the rest are gears that must turn whatever amount the free knobs force.
atoms.visual: Orange free knobs q₁ (n−k of them) and blue slaved dials q₂ (k of them) connected by a gearbox labeled −A₂⁻¹A₁; turning an orange knob spins the blue dials automatically.

atoms.label: Eq (6.9)
atoms.idea: Substituting δq₂ and using that δq₁ is free gives n−k equations: (d/dt ∂L/∂q̇₁ − ∂L/∂q₁ − Υ₁) − A₁ᵀA₂⁻ᵀ(d/dt ∂L/∂q̇₂ − ∂L/∂q₂ − Υ₂) = 0.
atoms.feynman: The slaved gears' resistance is reflected back through the gearbox onto your free knobs.
atoms.visual: Blue residual of q₂ travels backward through the gearbox (arrow flows −A₂⁻ᵀ then A₁ᵀ) and adds to the orange q₁ residual; the sum bar is held at zero.

atoms.idea: (6.9) is second order in (q₁,q₂); reuse the constraint q̇₂ = −A₂⁻¹A₁q̇₁ to remove q̇₂, q̈₂, and recover q₂ by integrating the constraint.
atoms.feynman: Once the free knobs' motion is known, the slaved dials just follow along — you replay them by counting gear turns.
atoms.visual: Run the reduced dynamics on orange knobs only; the blue dials are updated each frame by the gearbox, leaving a dotted blue track.

atoms.label: Ex 6.2
atoms.idea: Example: a disk rolling on a plane, configuration = planar position plus angles (continued).
atoms.feynman: A coin rolling on a table.
atoms.visual: A blue coin standing on a slate floor; drag to spin it off rolling.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Rolling disk: configuration (x,y,θ,φ), torque inputs, no-slip constraints (6.10), unconstrained kinetic-energy Lagrangian, Lagrange–d'Alembert form, and δx, δy solved in terms of δφ (6.11).

atoms.label: Fig 6.2
atoms.idea: Figure: an upright disk on a plane with contact point (x,y), heading angle and rolling angle marked.
atoms.feynman: A coin on its edge, seen from above: where it touches, which way it faces, how far it has turned.
atoms.visual: 3D: blue coin on a slate floor; teal contact dot at (x,y); a green-tinted heading arc θ on the floor and a blue spin marker φ on the rim.

atoms.idea: q = (x, y, θ, φ), radius ρ; inputs are two torques: one about the rolling axle and one steering about the vertical.
atoms.feynman: You can push a coin to roll it faster, and twist it to change its direction — two knobs.
atoms.visual: Two orange torque sliders (drive, steer) beside the coin; four readouts x,y,θ,φ.

atoms.label: Eq (6.10)
atoms.idea: Rolling without slip (like a fingertip rolling on an object): ẋ = ρ cosθ φ̇, ẏ = ρ sinθ φ̇, i.e. A(q)q̇ = 0 with two independent rows; the disk moves along its heading at the speed its rim turns.
atoms.feynman: A bike wheel: it only goes where it points, and it goes exactly as far as the tire rolls out.
atoms.visual: Coral bar across the coin (no sideways slide) and a lime arrow along the heading whose length is locked to the rim's spin rate; a slip meter stays at 0.

atoms.idea: Lagrangian = kinetic energy ignoring constraints: ½m(ẋ²+ẏ²) + ½I₁θ̇² + ½I₂φ̇² with the two disk inertias.
atoms.feynman: A coin's energy is its sliding energy plus its two kinds of spinning energy.
atoms.visual: Three gold energy bars (translation, steer-spin, roll-spin) summing into one total bar.

atoms.label: Eq (6.11)
atoms.idea: Lagrange–d'Alembert: (M q̈ − (0,0,τ_θ,τ_φ))·δq = 0 for δq with A δq = 0; the constraints give δx = ρ cosθ δφ, δy = ρ sinθ δφ.
atoms.feynman: Any tiny legal nudge of the coin is "turn it a bit" and "roll it a bit"; the slide is fixed by the roll.
atoms.visual: Ghost coins nudged by δθ, δφ (orange); the matching δx, δy (blue) are computed and drawn automatically from the gearbox ρ(cosθ, sinθ).

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Rolling disk: eliminating δx, δy gives (6.12); differentiating the constraints (6.13) yields decoupled 2×2 dynamics in (θ,φ) (6.14) plus first-order equations for x,y. Then §1.4 opens on non-integrable constraints.

atoms.label: Eq (6.12)
atoms.idea: With δθ, δφ free, two equations remain: I₁θ̈ = τ_θ, and mρ(cosθ ẍ + sinθ ÿ) + I₂φ̈ = τ_φ.
atoms.feynman: Turning the coin only fights its turning inertia; rolling it has to also drag the coin's mass forward.
atoms.visual: Two orange torque sliders each feed a bar; the roll bar shows an extra blue "mass dragged forward" chunk.

atoms.label: Eq (6.13)–(6.14)
atoms.idea: Differentiate constraints: ẍ = ρ cosθ φ̈ − ρ sinθ θ̇φ̇, ÿ = ρ sinθ φ̈ + ρ cosθ θ̇φ̇; substituting gives diag(I₁, I₂ + mρ²)(θ̈, φ̈) = (τ_θ, τ_φ), independent of x,y here (not true in general).
atoms.feynman: A rolling coin feels heavier to spin because spinning it also pushes its whole body forward: its rolling inertia gets the extra mρ².
atoms.visual: Blue inertia bar for rolling grows by a lime chunk mρ²; drag the radius ρ slider and that chunk swells quadratically. Same torque → slower spin-up.

atoms.idea: Positions follow from ẋ = ρ cosθ φ̇, ẏ = ρ sinθ φ̇. Splitting into second-order reduced equations plus first-order constraint equations is the signature of nonholonomic systems.
atoms.feynman: Know how the coin turned and rolled, then trace its path on the table like a pen on its edge.
atoms.visual: Run (θ,φ) dynamics with orange torque sliders; the pink (x,y) trail is drawn on the floor by integrating the constraint; replays from the same (θ,φ) history always give the same trail.

atoms.idea: Subsection 6.1.4 heading: the nature of nonholonomic constraints.

This machinery handles Pfaffian constraints without integrating them; for integrable ones it matches the minimal-coordinate answer, and for non-integrable ones the constraints must be inserted correctly.
atoms.feynman: A recipe that works whether or not the shortcut exists — but you must add the ingredients in the right order.
atoms.visual: Two cards: "holonomic" (lime) and "nonholonomic" (coral); both feed into the same Lagrange–d'Alembert machine icon and yield equations; for the coral card an order arrow (L → LdA → constrain) glows.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Substituting nonholonomic constraints into the Lagrangian before applying Lagrange's equations is wrong; a 3-variable example with ṡ = −aᵀ(r)ṙ shows the extra terms (6.15).

atoms.idea: Goal: show how non-integrable constraints affect mechanics and what goes wrong if handled carelessly.
atoms.feynman: Let's see what breaks if you take a shortcut with a rule that only governs speeds.
atoms.visual: The two-twin setup is introduced: lime and coral skates at the same start.

atoms.idea: Common error: plug the nonholonomic constraint into the Lagrangian and then use Lagrange's equations; correct procedure: unconstrained L → Lagrange–d'Alembert → then apply constraints.
atoms.feynman: Like baking: mixing eggs into flour before you've measured everything gives a different cake than following the steps.
atoms.visual: Two pipelines of tiles: lime [L] → [LdA] → [constrain]; coral [constrain] → [L] → [Lagrange]. The output trails of the two skates diverge.

atoms.idea: Test case: q=(r,s) ∈ R²×R, constraint ṡ + aᵀ(r)ṙ = 0, L(r,ṙ,ṡ), all independent of s. Constrained Lagrangian L_c(r,ṙ) = L(r, ṙ, −aᵀ(r)ṙ).
atoms.feynman: Two driving knobs r and one follower s that is told how fast to move by the knobs.
atoms.visual: Orange r₁,r₂ knobs, blue s dial driven by a gearbox a(r) that changes as you move; L_c drawn as an energy bar computed with the follower already slaved.

atoms.label: Eq (6.15)
atoms.idea: Applying Lagrange to L_c and expanding with the chain rule: left side = the correct Lagrange–d'Alembert expression; right side = (∂L/∂ṡ)(ȧᵢ − Σⱼ (∂aⱼ/∂rᵢ) ṙⱼ), generally nonzero.
atoms.feynman: Using the shortcut leaves an extra "ghost push" equal to how much the gearbox twists as you move.
atoms.visual: The coral twin carries a ghost coral arrow equal to the RHS of (6.15); its length is computed from ∂a/∂r and ṙ; the gap between lime and coral trails grows with this arrow.

atoms.idea: The left side of (6.15) is exactly the Lagrange–d'Alembert equation; the right side is spurious, introduced by substituting the constraints.
atoms.feynman: The correct answer plus an unwanted extra — the extra is the mistake.
atoms.visual: Equation strip: lime left block, coral right block flashing; drag the coral block away and the coral twin snaps onto the lime twin's path.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: If the constraint is a gradient (aᵢ = ∂h/∂rᵢ) the spurious terms vanish because mixed partials commute, so substitution is fine for holonomic constraints. §6.2 begins: hand dynamics from finger dynamics (6.16) plus object Newton–Euler.

atoms.idea: Conclusion: in general substituting Pfaffian constraints into L and then applying the Lagrange–d'Alembert equations gives the wrong dynamics.
atoms.feynman: Shortcut = wrong answer, unless the rule is secretly a place rule.
atoms.visual: Coral ✖ stamped on the coral twin's diverged trail.

atoms.idea: If aᵢ = ∂h/∂rᵢ, the RHS of (6.15) becomes (∂L/∂ṡ)(Σⱼ ∂²h/∂rᵢ∂rⱼ ṙⱼ − Σⱼ ∂²h/∂rⱼ∂rᵢ ṙⱼ) = 0 since mixed partials are equal, so substituting holonomic constraints gives the right equations.
atoms.feynman: Walking around a hill: if the rule is "track your height", going east-then-north or north-then-east lands at the same height, so nothing extra builds up.
atoms.visual: Staircase: (1) toggle a = ∇h; (2) two coral tiles ∂²h/∂rᵢ∂rⱼ and ∂²h/∂rⱼ∂rᵢ appear; (3) they slide together and annihilate with a lime flash; (4) ghost arrow shrinks to 0 and the twins' trails coincide.

atoms.idea: Section 6.2 heading: robot hand dynamics.
Use the constrained Lagrange machinery for robots cooperating on a task: first a hand manipulating an object, then other systems.
atoms.feynman: Same recipe for fingers on a ball, two arms on a box, or legs on the ground.
atoms.visual: Carousel of three icons — hand + ball, two arms + box, legged robot on ground — each with teal contact dots and lime constraint links.

atoms.idea: Subsection 6.2.1 heading: derivation and properties.

atoms.label: Eq (6.16)
atoms.idea: Hand dynamics = fingers + object joined by the grasp constraint. Fingers: M_f(θ)θ̈ + C_f θ̇ + N_f = τ with θ ∈ Rⁿ all joints, M_f, C_f block-diagonal and N_f stacked over the k fingers.
atoms.feynman: Each finger is its own little arm with its own heaviness; put them in one list and you have the whole hand.
atoms.visual: Fingers shown separately, each with a blue inertia block; the blocks slide into a block-diagonal M_f matrix (empty off-diagonal slate tiles = fingers don't feel each other directly).

atoms.idea: The object obeys Newton–Euler in its body frame: [mI 0; 0 I](v̇,ω̇) + (ω×mv, ω×Iω) = F^b.
atoms.feynman: A tossed box: push makes it speed up, and spinning boxes wobble on their own.
atoms.visual: Blue box floating with velocity (blue) and spin (red/green/blue) arrows; apply a pink wrench and watch v̇, ω̇; the ω×Iω wobble shown as a tumbling top.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Object Newton–Euler with gravity (6.17), rewritten in local coordinates with the same M/C/N structure; grasp constraint (6.18) and the three standing assumptions: force-closure & manipulable, invertible J_h, forces inside friction cones.

atoms.label: Eq (6.17)
atoms.idea: Body velocity V^b=(v,ω), wrench F^b, mass m, inertia I at the center of mass, pose x_o=(p,R). Under gravity alone the object equation gains a term Rᵀ(m g) and a Coriolis-like block built from ω.
atoms.feynman: A dropped box: it falls because of gravity, and if it's spinning it keeps wobbling the same way.
atoms.visual: Blue box with a slate gravity arrow rotated into the box frame (it swings around as the box tumbles); toggle the spin and see the ω-coupling term as a curling arrow.

atoms.idea: Because Lagrange–d'Alembert needs Rⁿ coordinates, write the object in local coordinates x ∈ R⁶: M_o(x)ẍ + C_o ẋ + N_o = 0, with M_o > 0 and Ṁ_o − 2C_o skew (Exercise 4).
atoms.feynman: Describe the box with six numbers so it looks just like a 6-jointed robot arm to the math.
atoms.visual: Box pose shown as six sliders (three position red/green/blue, three angles); the same blue M/C/N card used for the fingers appears for the object, making the two look alike.

atoms.label: Eq (6.18)
atoms.idea: Fingers and object are linked by the grasp constraint J_h(θ,x)θ̇ = Gᵀ(θ,x)ẋ in local coordinates.
atoms.feynman: Fingertips glued to the box: tips move exactly as the box's touching spots move.
atoms.visual: Snap the grasp: teal contact dots lock; each pair (pink fingertip velocity, blue object-point velocity) is shown overlapping.

atoms.idea: Assumption 1: force-closure and manipulable everywhere: G(FC) = Rᵖ and range(Gᵀ) ⊆ range(J_h).
atoms.feynman: The fingers can push the box any way you like and can follow the box anywhere it's moved.
atoms.visual: Teal friction cones at contacts; summed pink wrench cone fills all of wrench space (lime check); then the box is dragged in random directions and fingers follow (second lime check).

atoms.idea: Assumption 2: J_h invertible — no redundant finger motions; exactly the DOFs the task needs.
atoms.feynman: Each finger has just enough joints — no extra wiggle and none missing.
atoms.visual: J_h drawn as a square tile; determinant meter nonzero; no null-space self-motion slider available (it's greyed).

atoms.idea: Assumption 3: contact forces stay in their friction cones always, so the grasp constraint keeps holding; ensuring this is the controller's job. Assumptions 1–2 are relaxed in §6.3.
atoms.feynman: Hold the glass firmly enough that it doesn't slip — that's your job, not physics'.
atoms.visual: Purple contact force arrows inside teal cones; if any arrow leaves its cone it flashes coral and the box slips out of the fingers.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Composite Lagrangian (6.19), projection with δθ = J_h⁻¹Gᵀδx to get the object-space equation (6.20), then the effective manipulator form M̃ẍ + C̃ẋ + Ñ = F (6.21)–(6.22).

atoms.label: Eq (6.19)
atoms.idea: Total Lagrangian L = ½θ̇ᵀM_fθ̇ + ½ẋᵀM_oẋ − V_f(θ) − V_o(x), with q = (θ,x).
atoms.feynman: Total energy of the hand-plus-box is just the fingers' energy plus the box's energy.
atoms.visual: Two gold energy bars (fingers, box) stacking into one total bar.

atoms.idea: Grasp constraint gives δθ = J_h⁻¹Gᵀδx. Substituting into the Lagrange–d'Alembert expression and moving J_h⁻¹Gᵀ across the inner product turns the finger residual into GJ_h⁻ᵀ(finger residual)·δx.
atoms.feynman: Any legal nudge of the box decides the finger nudge; so you can carry the fingers' resistance over to the box with the same gearbox, run backwards.
atoms.visual: Staircase: (1) nudge the box by δx (blue ghost); (2) finger ghosts follow by J_h⁻¹Gᵀ (orange); (3) the finger residual arrow travels back from joints to box via J_h⁻ᵀ then G, landing as a pink wrench on the box.

atoms.label: Eq (6.20)
atoms.idea: With δx free: (object residual) + GJ_h⁻ᵀ(finger residual) = GJ_h⁻ᵀτ. Together with (6.18), this fully describes the system: n−m second-order rows plus m first-order rows.
atoms.feynman: Box's needs plus fingers' needs, both measured at the box, must equal what the motors push at the box.
atoms.visual: Balance scale at the box: left pan holds blue object residual + reflected orange finger residual; right pan holds the motor torques mapped into a pink wrench GJ_h⁻ᵀτ.

atoms.label: Eq (6.21)–(6.22)
atoms.idea: Using the split Lagrangian and eliminating θ̇, θ̈: M̃ẍ + C̃ẋ + Ñ = F with M̃ = M_o + GJ_h⁻ᵀM_fJ_h⁻¹Gᵀ, C̃ = C_o + GJ_h⁻ᵀ(C_fJ_h⁻¹Gᵀ + M_f d/dt(J_h⁻¹Gᵀ)), Ñ = N_o + GJ_h⁻ᵀN_f, F = GJ_h⁻ᵀτ.
atoms.feynman: Holding a box makes it feel heavier: your arms' heaviness gets added to the box's.
atoms.visual: The box's blue inertia ellipse grows by the orange finger ellipses pulled through J_h⁻¹Gᵀ; move the fingers to a stretched posture and the added part changes shape. τ sliders map to the pink F wrench at the box.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: The hand+object equations look like a single arm's (effective mass, Coriolis, gravity); Lemma 6.1 proves M̃ > 0 and dM̃/dt − 2C̃ skew; the result transfers back to SE(3) form (6.23). §2.2 internal forces begins.

atoms.idea: The system now looks like one open-chain arm: M̃ effective mass, C̃ effective Coriolis, Ñ effective gravity/friction; finger details are hidden inside them.
atoms.feynman: To the box, the whole hand feels like one big robot arm holding it.
atoms.visual: Fade the fingers to ghosts; the box keeps moving the same way with only its fat effective-inertia ellipse visible.

atoms.label: Lemma 6.1
atoms.idea: Properties: M̃ is symmetric positive definite and dM̃/dt − 2C̃ is skew-symmetric.
atoms.feynman: The box always resists being pushed (never "negative heavy"), and the speed-mixing forces never create energy.
atoms.visual: Two meters: min eigenvalue of M̃ always > 0 (lime); and xᵀ(dM̃/dt − 2C̃)x always 0 for random x arrows.

atoms.idea: Proof: positive definiteness follows from the definition given the grasp assumptions and injective J_h. Expanding dM̃/dt − 2C̃ gives skew pieces (object and finger skew terms reflected through GJ⁻ᵀ) plus a pair of terms that flip sign under transpose by symmetry of M_f.
atoms.feynman: Each piece of the hand separately doesn't create energy; gluing them with a gearbox doesn't either — the gearbox's extra terms come in a mirrored pair that cancels.
atoms.visual: Staircase: (1) M̃ ellipse = blue object ellipse + reflected finger ellipse, both positive; (2) skew tile for object, skew tile for fingers (lime); (3) the leftover pair shown as a tile and its mirror image across the diagonal, colored + and −; transpose flips them so they sum to a skew tile.

atoms.label: Eq (6.23)
atoms.idea: Since Lagrange–d'Alembert needs Euclidean coordinates, the derivation used local coordinates for SE(3); afterwards one can return to the global form M̃V̇^b + C̃V^b + Ñ = F^b with global inertia data (proof left as exercise).
atoms.feynman: Use a flat map to do the sums, then redraw the answer on the globe.
atoms.visual: A local chart patch (slate grid) on a blue SE(3) blob; derive on the grid, then the arrows lift back onto the blob as body velocity/wrench arrows.

atoms.idea: Subsection 6.2.2 heading: internal forces.
Recall: a force-closure grasp admits internal forces — contact forces producing zero net wrench on the object.
atoms.feynman: Squeezing a ball between two hands: lots of push, but the ball doesn't move.
atoms.visual: Two fingertips press a blue box with equal purple opposing arrows; the net-wrench arrow at the box center stays at zero length.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Internal forces enter through F = GJ_h⁻ᵀτ (null space of G) but also through the constraint forces themselves; the full (θ,x) equations (6.24) show λ are contact forces, computable from (6.25) or from finger dynamics.

atoms.idea: In F = GJ_h⁻ᵀτ, torques with J_h⁻ᵀτ in the null space of G produce no net wrench.
atoms.feynman: Some motor efforts only squeeze; they don't move the box.
atoms.visual: Orange torque slider along the "squeeze" direction: purple tip forces grow, pink net wrench stays zero.

atoms.label: Eq (6.24)
atoms.idea: Internal forces can also come from constraint forces dropped by Lagrange–d'Alembert. Full equations with A = [−J_h Gᵀ]: block-diag(M_f, M_o)q̈ + block-diag(C_f, C_o)q̇ + (N_f, N_o) + (−J_hᵀ; G)λ = (τ; 0).
atoms.feynman: Write the fingers and the box as separate bodies, with an invisible hand-shake force between them at each contact.
atoms.visual: Exploded view: fingers and box apart; purple λ arrows at each teal contact, pointing one way on the fingertip and the opposite way on the box (−J_hᵀλ and Gλ).

atoms.idea: So the multipliers λ are the contact forces, applied equal-and-opposite at fingertips and object; any component of λ in the null space of G is an internal force.
atoms.feynman: The invisible hand-shake force is exactly how hard each fingertip presses the box.
atoms.visual: Decompose λ: purple arrows split into a lime "moves the box" part and a teal "pure squeeze" part (null space of G).

atoms.label: Eq (6.25)
atoms.idea: λ = (AM̄⁻¹Aᵀ)⁻¹[AM̄⁻¹((τ,0) − C̄q̇ − N̄) + Ȧq̇]; projecting onto null(G) gives internal forces — messy, so in practice dynamic internal forces are ignored or measured by contact sensors.
atoms.feynman: You could calculate how hard the fingers squeeze while moving, but it's easier to just feel it with fingertip sensors.
atoms.visual: Live computation runs the formula and shows the purple arrows; a teal "sensor" icon at each tip shows the same numbers; toggle to "sensor-only" mode.

atoms.idea: If J_h invertible: λ = J_h⁻ᵀ(τ − M_fθ̈ − C_fθ̇ − N_f). So during motion, internal forces can arise from the dynamic terms even if J_h⁻ᵀτ has no squeeze part; λ = J_h⁻ᵀτ only at rest.
atoms.feynman: Swing a held cup quickly and your fingers squeeze harder on their own, even if you meant only to move it.
atoms.visual: Split bar for internal force: orange "commanded" (from τ) vs blue "dynamic" (from Mθ̈+Cθ̇+N). Shake the grasp fast and the blue part grows; pause and it drops to zero.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: The whole analysis assumes the grasp holds; contact forces must stay in friction cones, a job for the controller. §2.3: any system with J(q)θ̇ = Gᵀ(q)ẋ gets arm-like dynamics, starting with coordinated lifting.

atoms.label: Fig 6.3
atoms.idea: Figure: several robots lifting one object together.
atoms.feynman: Movers carrying a sofa together.
atoms.visual: Two orange-jointed arms on slate bases, both gripping a blue beam; teal welded contacts.

atoms.idea: Contact forces come from the constraints; if they leave the friction cone the constraints fail and (6.24) no longer applies, so a key control task is keeping them inside.
atoms.feynman: The model is only true while your grip holds; if the glass slips, all bets are off.
atoms.visual: Purple contact arrows with teal cones; a coral alarm when an arrow exits; the box then slides and the equation card greys out.

atoms.idea: Subsection 6.2.3 heading: other robot systems.
Any robot system with constraint J(q)θ̇ = Gᵀ(q)ẋ, q = (θ,x), automatically gets dynamics with the same form and structure as one open chain.
atoms.feynman: Fingers, arms, or anything gripping a common thing — same recipe.
atoms.visual: Template card "J θ̇ = Gᵀ ẋ" with three skins swiped through: hand, lifting team, welding arm.

atoms.idea: Coordinated lifting: several robots firmly grasp one object and can apply any wrench; each is a "finger" with full contact basis B = I and friction cone all of Rᵖ.
atoms.feynman: A firm handshake: you can push, pull and twist in any direction.
atoms.visual: Each grip shows a full lime sphere instead of a teal cone (any wrench allowed). Lift the beam with a gold target; the arms move together.

pages.summary: Coordinated lifting constraint: stacked inverse-adjoint-times-Jacobian blocks on the left, inverse adjoints of object-to-tool on the right; then workspace dynamics: describe the task directly in end-effector coordinates (welding example).

atoms.label: Fig 6.4
atoms.idea: Photo: an industrial robot doing arc welding.
atoms.feynman: A robot drawing a line of melted metal like icing on a cake.
atoms.visual: A single orange-jointed arm with a pink torch tip tracing a gold seam on a slate plate.

atoms.idea: Identifying contact and tool frames: J = blockdiag(Ad⁻¹_{g_{s_i t_i}} J^s_{s_i t_i}), Gᵀ = stack(Ad⁻¹_{g_{o t_i}}), giving J θ̇ = GᵀV^b_po; dynamics follow as in grasping.
atoms.feynman: Each mover's hand velocity must equal the sofa's velocity seen at the place they hold it.
atoms.visual: For each arm, a pink tool-frame twist and the blue object twist transported to that grip (adjoint), shown overlapping.

atoms.idea: Workspace dynamics: many tasks (e.g. welding) are naturally stated in tool pose; instead of solving inverse kinematics for a joint path, write dynamics in workspace coordinates.
atoms.feynman: Tell the pen where to go on the paper, not how each finger bone should bend.
atoms.visual: Drag the gold tool target directly; no joint sliders are shown — joints follow automatically.

atoms.idea: Use local coordinates: g: Q → Rᵖ forward kinematics, J = ∂g/∂θ square and nonsingular.
atoms.feynman: A map from joint knobs to tool position, with a square "how much it moves" table you can undo.
atoms.visual: Arm with p = n joints; J shown as a square tile with a nonzero determinant meter.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Workspace dynamics (6.26): J θ̇ = ẋ is the canonical constraint with G = I, giving M̃ = M_o + J⁻ᵀM_fJ⁻¹ etc.; inertia seen at the tool blows up near singularities, though joint dynamics stay fine; variants; no internal forces since G = I.

atoms.idea: Held object (e.g. welder) has M_o ẍ + C_o ẋ + N_o = 0 in workspace coordinates x ∈ Rᵖ with the usual structural properties.
atoms.feynman: The torch itself has some heft that the arm must carry.
atoms.visual: Small blue inertia ellipse at the pink torch tip.

atoms.label: Eq (6.26)
atoms.idea: J(θ)θ̇ = ẋ is the canonical constraint with G = I, so M̃ẍ + C̃ẋ + Ñ = F with M̃ = M_o + J⁻ᵀM_fJ⁻¹, C̃ = C_o + J⁻ᵀ(C_fJ⁻¹ + M_f d/dt J⁻¹), Ñ = N_o + J⁻ᵀN_f, F = J⁻ᵀτ; M̃ > 0 and skew property hold.
atoms.feynman: Push the tool and it feels as heavy as the tool plus the whole arm behind it.
atoms.visual: At the tip, the blue ellipse M̃ = tool ellipse + arm ellipse reflected through J⁻¹; joint torque sliders map to a pink force at the tip by J⁻ᵀ.

atoms.idea: M̃ is the system inertia seen from the tool. Near a singularity it grows unbounded (big tip forces, tiny tip accelerations) — an artifact of workspace coordinates; joint-space dynamics never become singular.
atoms.feynman: Pushing a door near its hinge: you shove hard and it barely moves, so it feels super heavy — but the door hasn't changed.
atoms.visual: Stretch the arm toward full extension: the tip's blue inertia ellipse balloons along the stretched direction toward ∞ (🚫 flash), while a side panel shows the joint-space inertia ellipse staying finite.

atoms.idea: Variants: use SE(3) with V^b and its derivative; drop the object (M_o, C_o, N_o = 0) to command an arm in end-effector coordinates; relax square J (treated in §6.3).
atoms.feynman: Same trick works with no tool, or with a twisty 3D pose instead of flat numbers.
atoms.visual: Three toggles: "no tool" (ellipse loses its small blue core), "3D pose" (tip frame with red/green/blue axes), "extra joints" (link to the Spare Joints scene).

atoms.idea: Unlike grasping, there are no internal forces here because G = I has no null space.
atoms.feynman: One hand on a stick can't squeeze it against itself.
atoms.visual: Internal-force slider is greyed; null-space-of-G readout shows dimension 0.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Hybrid position/force dynamics: a holonomic task constraint h(θ,x)=0 (chalk on a board) differentiated into J θ̇ = Gᵀẋ form (6.28); internal forces = torques pushing against the surface; effective dynamics with the object folded into the robot.

atoms.idea: Hybrid tasks: move along some directions while pushing in others, e.g. chalk on a board (motion in-plane, force into it); earlier sketched in Chapter 4, now treated with constrained dynamics.
atoms.feynman: Writing on a chalkboard: slide the chalk sideways while pressing it into the board.
atoms.visual: Slate board, pink chalk tip; a lime in-plane motion arrow and a purple push-into-board arrow, each with its own slider.

atoms.label: Eq (6.27)
atoms.idea: Model the task as holonomic h(θ,x) = 0, with x ∈ Rᵖ parameterizing allowed motions (chalk position and orientation on the board); h is a p-dim surface in configuration space; the task is motion along it and force against it.
atoms.feynman: The board is a wall your hand has to stay on; you choose where on the wall and how hard to press.
atoms.visual: A gold surface (the board) in the arm's configuration space; the tip slides on it with orange x sliders; a purple normal arrow pushes into it.

atoms.label: Eq (6.28)
atoms.idea: Differentiate: (∂h/∂θ)θ̇ = −(∂h/∂x)ẋ, i.e. J = ∂h/∂θ, Gᵀ = −∂h/∂x. Assume J square, nonsingular. Internal forces are torques with GJ⁻ᵀτ = 0 — exactly those pushing against the surface.
atoms.feynman: Pushing straight into the board doesn't move the chalk; it only presses harder.
atoms.visual: Torque sliders along the null space of GJ⁻ᵀ: chalk stays put, purple press arrow grows; torques outside it slide the chalk.

atoms.idea: Fold any held object into the robot model; then M̃ẍ + C̃ẋ + Ñ = F with M̃ = GJ⁻ᵀM_fJ⁻¹Gᵀ, C̃ = GJ⁻ᵀ(C_fJ⁻¹Gᵀ + M_f d/dt(J⁻¹Gᵀ)), Ñ = GJ⁻ᵀN_f (+ object terms), F = GJ⁻ᵀτ — because x needn't be any object's configuration.
atoms.feynman: The chalk's position on the board isn't a separate toy; it's just a way to say where the hand is.
atoms.visual: Blue effective-inertia ellipse drawn in the board's plane only (2D), computed from the arm's inertia reflected through J⁻¹Gᵀ.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Hybrid case wrap-up (internal forces don't affect motion; variants), then §6.3 opens: relax the square, invertible J_h assumption — too many joints (internal motions) or too few (can't follow contacts).

atoms.idea: Reason for folding the object in: for a chalkboard only two linear velocities are in ẋ; a curved board makes object dynamics in x messy.
atoms.feynman: On a curved board, describing the chalk as its own floating thing gets complicated; easier to treat it as part of the arm.
atoms.visual: Board toggle flat ↔ curved; on curved, the lime motion direction bends with the surface while the ellipse stays tangent.

atoms.idea: Internal (pressing) forces don't change the motion and can be ignored for free motion; to regulate them, solve for the Lagrange multipliers.
atoms.feynman: How hard you press the chalk doesn't change where it goes; but if you care about the pressure, you can measure it.
atoms.visual: Change the press slider: the pink chalk trail is identical; a purple λ gauge shows the press.

atoms.idea: Variants: subgroups of SE(3) with proper velocity interpretation; tasks specified directly by J and G rather than a holonomic h.
atoms.feynman: You can describe the rule by a surface or directly by "which ways may I move".
atoms.visual: Toggle between gold surface view and direct lime/coral direction-fan view of the same task.

atoms.idea: Section 6.3 heading: redundant and nonmanipulable robot systems.
So far each finger had exactly the DOFs its contact type needs (1 frictionless point, 3 point-with-friction, 4 soft finger), i.e. J_h square and invertible; now that assumption is dropped.
atoms.feynman: Up to now every finger had exactly enough joints; real hands may have more or fewer.
atoms.visual: Contact-type picker (frictionless/point/soft) shows the needed DOF count; the finger's joint count is a slider; J_h tile turns square (lime) only when they match.
atoms.beat: ➕ too many or too few joints

atoms.idea: Two failure modes: too many DOFs (dependent columns of J_h → internal motions with contacts fixed) and too few (J_h not full row rank → fingers can't follow all contact motions, possibly even when manipulable). Both can occur together; the fix is to add or drop task variables.
atoms.feynman: A snake arm can wiggle while its nose stays still; a stubby arm can't reach everywhere the box needs to go.
atoms.visual: Two panels: left, a 3-link finger whose elbow swings while the tip stays on a teal contact (lime self-motion trail); right, a 1-joint finger that can't follow the box when dragged sideways (coral gap).
atoms.beat: ➕ too many or too few joints

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Constraints themselves can create redundancy (soft-finger contacts on a 6-DOF finger); kinematic redundancy = null(J_h), actuator redundancy = null(G). For a lone redundant arm commanded in task space, J is wide, so complete it with K whose rows span null(J).

atoms.idea: Fix: add or remove task variables to fit the earlier framework.
atoms.feynman: If the snake arm has spare wiggle, give that wiggle its own knob.
atoms.visual: An extra orange "wiggle" knob appears next to the task sliders for the redundant arm.
atoms.beat: ➕ too many or too few joints

atoms.idea: The ideas apply to many constrained systems beyond hands; some variants are exercises.
atoms.feynman: Same trick for any team of linked robots.
atoms.visual: Icons for hand, two-arm team and legged robot each get the extra wiggle knob.
atoms.beat: ➕ too many or too few joints

atoms.idea: Subsection 6.3.1 heading: dynamics of redundant manipulators.
With constraints, a manipulator can be redundant with fewer than seven DOFs: e.g. a 6-DOF finger on a soft-finger contact has two spare DOFs (it can roll two ways without moving the object).
atoms.feynman: Press your fingertip on a table: you can rock the finger two ways while the table doesn't notice.
atoms.visual: A 6-joint finger pressing a blue object at a teal soft contact; two orange spare knobs rock the finger about the contact while the object stays perfectly still.
atoms.beat: ➕ too many or too few joints

atoms.idea: Two kinds of redundancy: kinematic (finger motions that don't move the object, null(J_h)) and actuator (finger forces that don't move it — internal forces, null(G)). Only kinematic is treated here.
atoms.feynman: Wiggling without moving the box (spare motion) vs squeezing without moving the box (spare force).
atoms.visual: Two-slot tray: left slot shows a lime elbow self-motion with frozen tip (null J_h); right slot shows purple squeeze arrows with zero net wrench (null G); the right slot dims to say "done earlier".

atoms.idea: Single redundant arm: in joint space nothing changes; but to command the end-effector directly, J ∈ R^{p×n} is wide so J⁻¹ doesn't exist and θ̇ can't be written from the tool velocity.
atoms.feynman: Many ways to reach the same cup — "where's my hand" doesn't tell you how your elbow is bent.
atoms.visual: 3-link arm, tip pinned on gold dot; ghost arms show a whole family of joint poses for the same tip; J drawn as a 2×3 wide tile with a coral "no inverse" badge.

atoms.idea: Choose K(θ) ∈ R^{(n−p)×n} whose rows span null(J); with J full row rank, K has constant rank n−p.
atoms.feynman: List the secret wiggles your arm can do without moving the hand.
atoms.visual: Null-space arrow(s) of J drawn in joint space (lime); stacking them as a K row under J.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Internal velocity v_N = Kθ̇ completes J to an invertible J̄ = [J; K], giving task-space dynamics in (ẋ, v_N); with orthonormal K ⊥ rows of J, J̄⁻¹ = [J⁺ Kᵀ]. v_N is a velocity, generally not the rate of any coordinate (Frobenius-style mixed-partial test). Example 6.3 begins.

atoms.idea: Define internal motion v_N := Kθ̇, so (ẋ, v_N) = J̄θ̇ with J̄ = [J; K] square.
atoms.feynman: Two dials for where the hand goes plus one dial for how the elbow is folded = one full set of instructions.
atoms.visual: J̄ tile becomes square 3×3; the (ẋ, ẏ, v_N) readout drives the arm uniquely; det(J̄) meter lime.

atoms.idea: J̄ invertible ⇒ M̃(ẍ, v̇_N) + C̃(ẋ, v_N) + Ñ = J̄⁻ᵀτ with M̃ = J̄⁻ᵀMJ̄⁻¹, C̃ = J̄⁻ᵀ(CJ̄⁻¹ + M d/dt J̄⁻¹), Ñ = J̄⁻ᵀN (G = I).
atoms.feynman: The arm now feels like a 3-knob machine: two knobs for the hand, one for the elbow.
atoms.visual: Inertia ellipsoid in (x, y, v_N) space drawn from J̄⁻ᵀMJ̄⁻¹; torque sliders map to a pink 3-vector J̄⁻ᵀτ.

atoms.idea: If K's rows are orthonormal and orthogonal to J's rows, J̄⁻¹ = [J⁺ Kᵀ] with J⁺ = Jᵀ(JJᵀ)⁻¹ the least-squares right inverse.
atoms.feynman: Choose the elbow knob to be "as different as possible" from the hand knobs, and undoing them becomes easy.
atoms.visual: In joint space: the row-space of J (pink plane) and the K line (lime) meet at a right angle; the inverse is drawn as J⁺ (shortest joint motion) plus Kᵀ v_N (pure wiggle).

atoms.idea: The internal motion is a velocity v_N, not a coordinate y: an h with ∂h/∂θ = K exists only if mixed partials match, ∂K_ij/∂θ_k = ∂K_ik/∂θ_j (Chapter 7 expands).
atoms.feynman: Counting your steps sideways doesn't always give a "sideways position" — walking in a loop can leave the count off.
atoms.visual: Drive a small closed loop in (ẋ, v_N) commands; with a non-integrable K the arm returns with tip home but joints shifted (coral gap in θ); with an integrable K the gap is zero (lime).

atoms.idea: Since a K that is an exact differential is hard to choose in general, no explicit coordinates for the internal motion are assumed; velocity relations suffice, and Lagrange–d'Alembert handles them.
atoms.feynman: Like describing a skate by its allowed pushes instead of a map of everywhere it can be.
atoms.visual: Same card icon as the Pfaffian scene (lime/coral fan) appears next to the K row, linking the two ideas.

atoms.label: Ex 6.3
atoms.idea: Example: a planar 3-link arm, unit links, absolute angles; tip (x, y) = (Σcosθᵢ, Σsinθᵢ).
atoms.feynman: Three sticks end to end; the tip is where you end up adding the three arrows.
atoms.visual: 3-link arm with orange joints, each link an arrow; pink tip = head of the arrow chain.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Example 6.3: J for the 3-link arm; K = [0 0 1] is a true coordinate (θ₃), valid when links 1–2 aren't aligned; an orthogonal choice of K fails the mixed-partials test, so its v_N is not a coordinate rate. Dynamics (6.29) in (x, y, v_N).

atoms.label: Fig 6.5
atoms.idea: Figure: 3-link planar arm with angles measured from the horizontal, base B and tip (x, y).
atoms.feynman: Three-piece folding ruler pinned at one end.
atoms.visual: Slate base, three blue links, orange joints with angle arcs measured from a horizontal red line.

atoms.idea: J(θ) = [−sinθ₁ −sinθ₂ −sinθ₃; cosθ₁ cosθ₂ cosθ₃].
atoms.feynman: Turning any link swings the tip at right angles to that link.
atoms.visual: Three small arrows at the tip, each ⟂ to its link, scaled by that joint's speed; the tip velocity is their sum.

atoms.idea: Choice K = [0 0 1] = ∂θ₃/∂θ: internal motion is the last link's angle (a real coordinate), valid unless θ₁ = θ₂.
atoms.feynman: Use the angle of the last stick as your elbow knob — a genuine position you can read.
atoms.visual: v_N slider rotates the last link while the first two re-fold to keep the tip on gold; loops give zero drift (lime). Aligning links 1 and 2 triggers a 🚫 flash.

atoms.idea: Choice K = [sin(θ₂−θ₃), −sin(θ₁−θ₃), sin(θ₁−θ₂)] (null of J, valid unless all aligned): ∂K₁/∂θ₂ = cos(θ₂−θ₃) ≠ −cos(θ₁−θ₃) = ∂K₂/∂θ₁, so no h exists and v_N is not a coordinate rate.
atoms.feynman: This elbow knob counts spins, but after a round trip the count doesn't match the shape: it's not a real position.
atoms.visual: Staircase: (1) two partial-derivative tiles computed live; (2) they show different numbers (coral ≠); (3) driving a closed loop in v_N and tip leaves a coral joint drift.

atoms.label: Eq (6.29)
atoms.idea: Ignoring gravity/friction, end-effector dynamics: J̄⁻ᵀMJ̄⁻¹(ẍ, ÿ, v̇_N) + (J̄⁻ᵀCJ̄⁻¹ + J̄⁻ᵀM d/dt J̄⁻¹)(ẋ, ẏ, v_N) = J̄⁻ᵀτ.
atoms.feynman: The same arm equation, just read in "hand and elbow" knobs instead of "joint" knobs.
atoms.visual: Live 3×3 effective-inertia matrix heat-map updating as the arm moves; push the tip with a pink force and watch v_N also respond through off-diagonal entries.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: J̄ for the 3-link example; general redundant grasps: augment J_h with K_h spanning null(J_h) so J̄_hθ̇ = Ḡᵀ(ẋ, v_N) with J̄_h invertible, giving dynamics (6.30). Augmenting is needed because x alone underdetermines the motion. Static force relations need care.

atoms.idea: Stacked J̄ for the example: J rows on top of the orthogonal K row.
atoms.feynman: Two rows for the hand, one for the elbow — a full instruction sheet.
atoms.visual: 3×3 tile with top two rows pink and bottom row lime; determinant meter.

atoms.label: Eq (6.30)
atoms.idea: General redundant grasp (force-closure, manipulable, null(J_h) ≠ 0): choose K_h spanning null(J_h); [J_h; K_h]θ̇ = blockdiag(Gᵀ, I)(ẋ, v_N). J̄_h is invertible, so M̃(ẍ, v̇_N) + C̃(ẋ, v_N) = ḠJ̄_h⁻ᵀτ with M̃ = ḠJ̄_h⁻ᵀMJ̄_h⁻¹Ḡᵀ, C̃ analogous.
atoms.feynman: Give every finger's spare wiggle its own knob next to the box's knobs, and the hand is back to the tidy case.
atoms.visual: Hand with a redundant finger: box pose sliders (blue) plus v_N knobs (orange); augmented block matrices drawn as tiles [J_h; K_h] and [Gᵀ 0; 0 I].

atoms.idea: Redundant systems fit the same framework; augmentation is needed because task variables x alone don't determine the motion; adding v_N completes the description.
atoms.feynman: Telling a puppet where its hand goes isn't enough; you must also say how its elbow bends.
atoms.visual: Ghost family of arms collapses to one arm the moment the v_N knob is set.

atoms.idea: Chapter 5's static joint-torque/contact-force/object-wrench relations need care in the redundant case.
atoms.feynman: The old "push this hard to hold that" rules need a footnote when there are spare joints.
atoms.visual: The static τ = J_hᵀf_c panel from the grasp scene appears with a coral asterisk.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Redundant grasp statics (6.31): τ = J_hᵀf_c + K_hᵀf_N; nonzero f_N makes internal motion and dynamic constraint forces, so static relations then fail. §3.2: nonmanipulable grasps (J_h not full row rank) — restrict object motion to what fingers can follow.

atoms.label: Eq (6.31)
atoms.idea: In twist form [J_h; K_h]θ̇ = blockdiag(Gᵀ, I)(V^b, v_N); quasistatic forces: τ = J_hᵀf_c + K_hᵀf_N, F^b = Gf_c, with f_N the forces dual to internal motions.
atoms.feynman: Motor effort splits into "pushing the box" plus "pushing the spare wiggle".
atoms.visual: Torque bar splits into a pink part J_hᵀf_c and an orange part K_hᵀf_N; the f_N slider is its own knob.

atoms.idea: With f_N = 0 you recover the usual relations. Nonzero f_N drives internal motion, which accelerates joints and can create constraint forces, so the full dynamics (6.30) must be used; non-redundant systems don't have this issue (fixed tip ⇒ fixed joints).
atoms.feynman: Push your elbow while your fingertip is on the table: your elbow moves, and that motion changes how hard your fingertip presses.
atoms.visual: Raise f_N: elbows start swinging (lime trail); contact force arrows (purple) wobble with the swing, and the static prediction (dashed) separates from the true value (solid).

atoms.idea: Subsection 6.3.2 heading: nonmanipulable grasps.
Now J_h lacks full row rank: some contact motions can't be tracked. Assume J_h full column rank (else augment as above).
atoms.feynman: A finger that can't bend sideways can't follow a box sliding sideways.
atoms.visual: Drag the box along a coral direction; the fingertip lags behind (coral gap at the teal contact).

atoms.idea: Usually this makes the grasp nonmanipulable; rarely J_h can be bijective onto range(Gᵀ) yet not onto all of Rᵐ (manipulable, nonredundant, not square) — ignored as practically rare.
atoms.feynman: Almost always "can't follow some motions" means "can't move the box every way" — rare exceptions exist.
atoms.visual: Range(Gᵀ) as a blue plane, range(J_h) as a pink plane; usually the blue plane pokes out of pink (coral sliver); a rare-case toggle shows them coinciding.

atoms.idea: Object motion must be restricted to what the fingers allow; structural forces inside the hand resist the other directions.
atoms.feynman: Like a door hinge: you can swing it, but the hinge pushes back if you try to lift it off.
atoms.visual: Push the box in a coral direction: a purple structural force inside the finger links pushes back, box doesn't budge.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Nonmanipulable grasp dynamics: W = allowed object velocities (constant dimension l), spanned by H; write ẋ = Hw and use J_h's pseudo-inverse to get M̃ẇ + C̃w + Ñ = F (6.33) plus ẋ = Hw (6.32). §3.3 SCARA example begins.

atoms.idea: Contacts are assumed maintained; keeping forces in friction cones is the controller's responsibility.
atoms.feynman: Still your job not to drop it.
atoms.visual: Teal friction cones with purple contact arrows, coral alarm on exit.

atoms.label: Eq (6.32)
atoms.idea: W(θ,x) = {ẋ : ∃θ̇, J_hθ̇ = Gᵀẋ} with constant dimension l > 0, varying smoothly; H ∈ R^{p×l} spans W, so J_hθ̇ = GᵀHw, ẋ = Hw with w ∈ Rˡ.
atoms.feynman: List only the ways the box can actually move, and steer with those few knobs.
atoms.visual: Velocity ball around the box: lime subspace W (a plane or line), coral rest; w sliders (orange) move the box only within lime.

atoms.label: Eq (6.33)
atoms.idea: J_h maps onto range(Ḡᵀ) with Ḡᵀ = GᵀH but may be non-square; use J_h⁺ = (J_hᵀJ_h)⁻¹J_hᵀ. Dynamics: M̃ẇ + C̃w + Ñ = F with M̃ = M_o + ḠJ_h⁺ᵀM_fJ_h⁺Ḡᵀ, etc., plus first-order ẋ = Hw.
atoms.feynman: Steer with the allowed knobs only; the hand's heaviness is added just along those directions.
atoms.visual: l-dimensional inertia ellipse inside the lime subspace; fingers driven by θ̇ = J_h⁺Ḡᵀw; a pink pose trail integrates ẋ = Hw.

atoms.idea: Subsection 6.3.3 heading: example, two-fingered SCARA grasp.
Example: two SCARA fingers grasping a box (Figure 6.6).
atoms.feynman: Two desk-lamp-style arms pinching a block.
atoms.visual: Two SCARA arms (three vertical-axis orange joints plus a slider) on slate bases; blue box between them.
atoms.beat: 🦾 two SCARA fingers hold a box

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: SCARA grasp: soft-finger contacts give an 8×8 J_h that is singular — rotation about the contact line is unreachable and the first three joints allow self-motion; augment with y = sums of each finger's first three joint angles (true coordinates).

atoms.label: Fig 6.6
atoms.idea: Figure: two SCARA robots at bases S1, S2 pinching a box of width 2r at contacts C1, C2, with link lengths and offsets.
atoms.feynman: Two robot arms reaching in from both sides to hold a box between their fingertips.
atoms.visual: Top-down + side views; teal contact frames at C1, C2 (red/green/blue axes), box frame O, base frames S1, S2.
atoms.beat: 🦾 two SCARA fingers hold a box

atoms.idea: Soft-finger contacts; constraint blockdiag(J_h1, J_h2)θ̇ = [G₁ᵀ; G₂ᵀ]V^b with 8 rows on each side.
atoms.feynman: Each fingertip must match the box's motion at its touch point, including twisting.
atoms.visual: Two 4×4 orange tiles on the diagonal of an 8×8 grid; two blue Gᵀ blocks stacked on the right.
atoms.beat: 🦾 two SCARA fingers hold a box

atoms.idea: J_h is square but singular: the grasp is not manipulable (rotation about the contact line violates soft-finger constraints the fingers can't match).
atoms.feynman: Pinch a coin between two fingertips: you can't make the coin roll about the pinch axis because your fingertips can't twist.
atoms.visual: Dashed gold line through the contacts; try to roll the box about it — coral 🚫 and the box locks.
atoms.beat: 🔄 spin about the contact line forbidden

atoms.idea: Internal motions: moving each finger's first three joints so the tip's xy stays fixed.
atoms.feynman: Each arm can fold its elbow in or out while its fingertip stays on the box.
atoms.visual: Elbow self-motion slider: lime elbow trails while pink tips stay glued.

atoms.idea: Augment with y = (θ₁₁+θ₁₂+θ₁₃, θ₂₁+θ₂₂+θ₂₃) (end-link heading, as in Ex 6.3) — a real coordinate, not just a velocity; augmented constraint is 10 rows × 8 columns.
atoms.feynman: Measure each arm's elbow fold by the direction its last link points — that's a number you can read anytime.
atoms.visual: Two orange y-dials showing each arm's last-link heading; augmented matrix grows two rows [1 1 1 0 | 0…] and [0… | 1 1 1 0].

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: SCARA: augmenting doesn't fix nonmanipulability; H removes the forbidden spin so w = (w′, y) ∈ R⁷ with a pseudo-inverse. §6.4 opens: tendon transmissions — relate tendon forces to joint torques, also elastic tendons driven by position actuators.

atoms.idea: Augmentation keeps the grasp nonmanipulable (J_h still doesn't cover range Gᵀ). Remove the bad direction: H′ selects five of the six object twist components (dropping rotation about the contact line), H = blockdiag(H′, I).
atoms.feynman: If the box can't roll that one way, stop asking it to: delete that knob.
atoms.visual: Six blue twist knobs for the box; the one aligned with the gold contact line greys out and is removed, leaving five plus the two orange y-dials.
atoms.beat: ✂️ cut the bad spin with H

atoms.idea: Section 6.4 heading: kinematics and statics of tendon actuation.
Direct joint motors are often too big for useful forces; transmissions (linkages, tendons, gears, pulleys) carry force from remote actuators to joints.
atoms.feynman: Your fingers have no muscles inside them — strings (tendons) run to muscles in your forearm.
atoms.visual: A finger with empty joints; strings run down to motor pucks in a slate "forearm" box.

atoms.idea: Tendon networks are light and flexible but complicate kinematics. Questions: how tendon-end forces map to joint torques, and (less common) elastic tendons driven by position-controlled motors.
atoms.feynman: Puppet strings: pulling one string moves the puppet's arm, but which way depends on how the string is threaded.
atoms.visual: Pull an orange force slider on a puck; the string tightens and joint torques appear as curved arrows; a second mode swaps force pucks for stepper-motor position dials with springy strings.
