pages.summary: Inelastic tendons: each cable runs from a force actuator to one link but pushes on every joint it wraps; routing is captured by extension functions h_i(θ), linear (l_i ± Σ r_ij θ_j) for simple pulleys, nonlinear for sheathed routings.

atoms.label: Fig 6.7
atoms.idea: Figure: a two-joint finger driven by four tendons h₁…h₄ over pulleys.
atoms.feynman: A puppet finger with four strings coming out of the bottom.
atoms.visual: Two orange joints with pulley wheels; four colored strings h₁–h₄ wrapping over/under them and ending in motor pucks at the base.

atoms.idea: Subsection 6.4.1 heading: inelastic tendons.

Setup: each tendon is an inextensible cable driven by a force source (e.g. DC motor), attached between base and a link or between two links, with no tendon-to-tendon connections; goal: tendon forces → joint torques.
atoms.feynman: Each string is pulled by its own motor and tied to one bone.
atoms.visual: Each puck has an orange force slider; strings are drawn as non-stretching lines (fixed length meter).

atoms.idea: Pulling one tendon can torque many joints because it presses against everything guiding it along its path; avoiding this coupling needs awkward routing.
atoms.feynman: Pull a string that runs over two pulleys and both pulleys feel it.
atoms.visual: Pull only the string to the fingertip: curved torque arrows appear on both joints (the inner one coral-tinted as "unwanted" coupling).

atoms.idea: Extension function h_i: Q → R = displacement of tendon end vs joint angles. For pulley networks h_i(θ) = l_i ± r_i1θ₁ ± … ± r_inθ_n; l_i nominal length, r_ij pulley radius, sign = whether the path lengthens with positive rotation.
atoms.feynman: Wind a string on a spool: turning the spool by an angle pays out radius × angle of string.
atoms.visual: Turn a joint: the string's tail slides into/out of its puck; a length bar shows h_i growing (lime) or shrinking (coral) at a rate set by the pulley radius r.

atoms.idea: Sheathed routings give nonlinear extensions; for Figure 6.8's top tendon, h₁ = l₁ + 2√(a²+b²)·cos(atan(a/b) + θ/2) − 2b for θ > 0.
atoms.feynman: A string passing over a bent elbow gets longer in a curvy, not straight-line, way.
atoms.visual: h₁(θ) plotted live as a curve vs θ next to a straight line for the pulley tendon; the elbow geometry with offsets a, b shown.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Second tendon of Fig 6.8 is linear (l₂ + Rθ); energy conservation with ė = Pᵀθ̇ gives τ = P f, P = (∂h/∂θ)ᵀ the coupling matrix (cousin of the grasp map); dynamics M θ̈ + Cθ̇ + N = P f, ignoring tendon/actuator dynamics.

atoms.label: Fig 6.8
atoms.idea: Figure: a joint with one tendon routed through offset sheaths (nonlinear extension) and one over a pulley of radius R (h₂ = l₂ + Rθ for θ > 0); roles swap for θ < 0.
atoms.feynman: Two strings over one knuckle: one runs round a wheel, the other zig-zags through little loops.
atoms.visual: One joint, two strings: one hugs a pulley (straight-line length chart), the other runs through sheaths at offsets a, b (curved chart); flip θ's sign and the two charts swap.

atoms.idea: Stack extensions e = h(θ) ∈ Rᵖ for p tendons; coupling matrix P(θ) = (∂h/∂θ)ᵀ ∈ R^{n×p}; then ė = Pᵀθ̇.
atoms.feynman: A table telling how much each string reels in for each joint you bend.
atoms.visual: Grid P with rows = joints, columns = tendons; entries light orange where a string wraps a joint; spinning a joint shows matching column entries feeding string-speed bars.

atoms.idea: Lossless: tendon power fᵀė equals joint power τᵀθ̇ for all θ̇, hence τ = P(θ)f. P plays the role the grasp map plays for contacts.
atoms.feynman: A pulley system can't create energy: what your hand puts into the rope comes out at the load.
atoms.visual: Two power meters (rope side f·ė and joint side τ·θ̇) always equal; side-by-side with the grasp map icon (fingertip forces → box wrench) to show the analogy.

atoms.idea: Combined: M(θ)θ̈ + C θ̇ + N = P(θ)f, valid if actuator and tendon dynamics are negligible (force passes instantly).
atoms.feynman: Pull the strings and the finger moves as if the motors were in its joints.
atoms.visual: Simulated 2-link finger: orange force sliders on pucks → torques Pf → the finger swings (RK4).

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Example 6.4: two-joint finger with four tendons through sheaths; extension functions per joint, coupling matrix P(θ) (nonlinear entry from the sheathed routing); outer-joint tendons also torque the inner joint. §4.2 elastic tendons begins.

atoms.label: Fig 6.9
atoms.idea: Figure: planar two-joint finger with tendons h₁–h₄ routed through sheaths along the links.
atoms.feynman: A finger with four strings running through little tubes along its sides.
atoms.visual: Two-link finger, sheaths drawn as teal loops on each link, four strings threaded through.

atoms.label: Ex 6.4
atoms.idea: Example: two revolute joints, four tendons in sheaths on the link sides.
atoms.feynman: Two knuckles, four strings.
atoms.visual: Four orange force pucks at the base, one per string.

atoms.idea: Inner-joint tendons over a pulley of radius R₁: h₂ = l₂ − R₁θ₁, h₃ = l₃ + R₁θ₁. Outer tendons: h₁ has the nonlinear sheath term in θ₁ minus R₂θ₂; h₄ = l₄ + R₁θ₁ + R₂θ₂ (θ₁ > 0; swapped for θ₁ < 0).
atoms.feynman: Add up how much each knuckle stretches or slackens each string.
atoms.visual: Four length bars, each split into colored chunks contributed by joint 1 and joint 2; bend each joint and watch which chunks change.

atoms.idea: P(θ) for θ₁ > 0: row 1 = (−√(a²+b²) sin(atan(a/b) + θ₁/2), −R₁, R₁, R₁); row 2 = (−R₂, 0, 0, R₂). Tendons 1 and 4, meant for the outer joint, also torque the inner joint.
atoms.feynman: The strings for the fingertip also bend the knuckle below — like pulling a sleeve string that runs past the elbow.
atoms.visual: 2×4 P grid; pull tendon 4 only: torque arrows on both joints, with joint-1 arrow highlighted as coupling. Entry (1,1) changes as θ₁ bends (it's nonlinear).

atoms.idea: Subsection 6.4.2 heading: elastic tendons.
Extend the analysis to elastic tendons, assuming they slide freely along the finger.
atoms.feynman: Now the strings are rubber bands instead of fishing line.
atoms.visual: Strings switch to a stretchy rendering (zig-zag spring at the base).

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Elastic tendons: lump elasticity in a base spring, tendon massless; force relations τ = Pf still hold. With position-controlled actuators, f = K(e + h(0) − h(θ)), giving dynamics with stiffness term S(θ) = PK(h(θ) − h(0)) and coupling Q = PK.

atoms.label: Fig 6.10
atoms.idea: Figure: planar finger with tendons whose ends e₁…e₄ are position-commanded through springs.
atoms.feynman: Each string has a spring at the bottom and a crank that winds it.
atoms.visual: Four orange position dials e₁–e₄, each feeding a slate spring then a string over the joints.

atoms.idea: Free sliding ⇒ all elasticity can be lumped in one spring at the tendon base; tendon massless (fast compared with the robot), so no tendon dynamics.
atoms.feynman: A long rubber band acts like one spring plus a weightless string.
atoms.visual: Toggle "distributed" vs "lumped": a string of tiny springs collapses into a single spring at the base, same tip behavior.

atoms.idea: Force relations from inelastic tendons still hold: a massless tendon stretches until its spring force equals the applied force, then transmits exactly that force.
atoms.feynman: Pull a rubber band tied to a box: it stretches a bit, but then pulls the box exactly as hard as you pull it.
atoms.visual: Apply an orange force: the spring stretches instantly to balance it, and the purple force at the joint end equals the applied force (two equal meters).

atoms.idea: Position control: actuator commands extension e_i; mechanism contributes h_i(θ); zero tension at θ = 0, e_i = 0. Tendon force f_i = k_i(e_i + h_i(0) − h_i(θ)).
atoms.feynman: Wind the crank to stretch the spring: the pull is stiffness × how far the spring is stretched.
atoms.visual: Turn dial e_i: spring stretches; purple force bar = k_i × stretch; bend the finger to lengthen the path and the stretch (and force) drops.

atoms.idea: With K = diag(k_i): f = K(e + h(0) − h(θ)), dynamics M θ̈ + Cθ̇ + N + PK(h(θ) − h(0)) = PKe. S(θ) := PK(h(θ) − h(0)) is the network's stiffness; Q := PK maps commanded extensions to torques.
atoms.feynman: The springy strings act like a spring inside each joint, plus knobs that set where that spring wants to rest.
atoms.visual: Joint-space panel: restoring torque arrow S(θ) pulling the finger back toward rest, and an orange arrow Qe from the dials; the finger settles where they balance.

pages.summary: With fixed inputs S(θ) is the restoring torque. Example 6.5: linear extensions give constant P, diagonal K, a symmetric 2×2 stiffness S(θ) and Q = PK. §4.3: tendon tensions must be positive, so torques lie in the positive span of P's columns.

atoms.idea: For constant inputs, S(θ) is the restoring torque when the finger is bent from equilibrium.
atoms.feynman: Push a springy finger and let go: it snaps back.
atoms.visual: Freeze the dials, drag the finger tip away, release: it oscillates back to the gold rest pose; S(θ) arrow points home.

atoms.idea: Force- and position-controlled tendons can be mixed (exercises).
atoms.feynman: Some strings pulled by hand, some by springs and cranks.
atoms.visual: Per-tendon toggle: force puck vs position dial + spring.

atoms.label: Ex 6.5
atoms.idea: Example: linear extensions h₁ = l₁ + r₁₁θ₁ − r₁₂θ₂, h₂ = l₂ − r₂₁θ₁, h₃ = l₃ + r₃₁θ₁, h₄ = l₄ − r₄₁θ₁ + r₄₂θ₂; so P = [r₁₁ −r₂₁ r₃₁ −r₄₁; −r₁₂ 0 0 r₄₂] is constant.
atoms.feynman: With round pulleys everywhere, the string-to-joint table never changes as the finger bends.
atoms.visual: P grid with numeric pulley radii; bend the finger and the grid stays frozen (lime "constant" badge).

atoms.idea: K = diag(k₁..k₄). Stiffness S(θ) = PK(h(θ) − h(0)) = PKPᵀθ: a symmetric 2×2 matrix with entries k₁r₁₁² + k₂r₂₁² + k₃r₃₁² + k₄r₄₁² , −k₁r₁₁r₁₂ − k₄r₄₁r₄₂ off-diagonal, k₁r₁₂² + k₄r₄₂².
atoms.feynman: Each string adds its own little spring to the joints, sized by stiffness × pulley radius squared.
atoms.visual: Joint-space stiffness ellipse PKPᵀ; each tendon's k_i slider makes the ellipse fatter along that tendon's column direction.

atoms.idea: Q = PK = [k₁r₁₁ −k₂r₂₁ k₃r₃₁ −k₄r₄₁; −k₁r₁₂ 0 0 k₄r₄₂] maps actuator extensions to joint torques.
atoms.feynman: Wind a crank one notch and this table says how much each knuckle gets twisted.
atoms.visual: Q grid; turn one dial and the matching column lights, with torque arrows at the joints.

atoms.idea: Subsection 6.4.3 heading: analysis and control of tendon-driven fingers.
Tendons can only pull: every tension must be strictly positive (continued).
atoms.feynman: You can pull a rope but you can't push it.
atoms.visual: Try to drag a tension slider below 0: the string goes slack (wavy coral line) and stops transmitting.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Achievable torques = positive span of P's columns (like frictionless contacts). Force-closure tendon network (6.34): P onto plus a strictly positive null vector. Carathéodory/Steinitz: n+1 ≤ tendons, 2n suffice (N+1 and 2N designs). Force-controlled solution f = P⁺τ + f_N; elastic case (6.35).

atoms.idea: Reachable torques form the positive span of P's columns — exactly like frictionless point contacts, so grasp tools apply.
atoms.feynman: Fingers that can only push on a box and strings that can only pull on joints obey the same arithmetic.
atoms.visual: Torque plane with orange column arrows of P; the positive cone they sweep is lime; the grasp icon (frictionless pushes) appears beside it with an identical cone.

atoms.label: Eq (6.34)
atoms.idea: Force-closure tendon network: every τ ∈ Rⁿ is Pf with all f_i > 0. Iff P is onto and some strictly positive f_N has Pf_N = 0.
atoms.feynman: Like tug-of-war teams balanced so the rope doesn't move but every rope is tight; from there you can nudge any way.
atoms.visual: Head-to-tail chain of P's columns scaled by a positive f_N closing into a loop (zero torque), then a gold target torque anywhere: the cone covers the whole plane (lime) — remove one tendon and a coral wedge appears.

atoms.idea: From Carathéodory and Steinitz (Chapter 5): an n-joint finger needs at least n+1 tendons, and more than 2n are redundant. Common designs: "N+1" (one shared tendon one way, n opposers) and "2N" (antagonistic pair per joint, used in the examples).
atoms.feynman: To steer two knuckles with strings you need at least three strings; four (two per knuckle, like biceps and triceps) is plenty.
atoms.visual: Toggle layouts: N+1 (three arrows spanning the plane with a closing loop) and 2N (two ± pairs); a counter shows tendons vs n+1 and 2n bounds.

atoms.idea: Force-controlled: f = P⁺(θ)τ + f_N, P⁺ = Pᵀ(PPᵀ)⁻¹, f_N ∈ null(P) with positive entries making every tension positive; choose f_N as small as possible (taut but not over-stressed).
atoms.feynman: First work out the pulls you need, then tighten every string just enough that none goes slack.
atoms.visual: Tension bars from P⁺τ (some coral negative); slide the preload f_N up: all bars lift together until the lowest crosses zero (lime) — that minimal preload is marked gold.

atoms.label: Eq (6.35)
atoms.idea: Elastic + position-controlled: solve PKe = τ with every stretch e_i + h_i(0) − h_i(θ) > 0; with K invertible and force-closure, some e_N > 0 has PKe_N = 0, so take e = (PK)⁺τ + e_N.
atoms.feynman: Same trick with cranks: wind every spring a little extra so none ever goes slack.
atoms.visual: Dials instead of force pucks: spring-stretch bars; raising e_N lifts all stretches above zero without changing the joint torque arrows.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Elastic preload e_N large enough satisfies (6.35); mixed and link-to-link tendons are exercises. §6.5: extend Chapter 4 controllers to hands — track object trajectory, then add internal force; dynamics M ẍ + Cẋ + N = GJ⁻ᵀτ with M > 0, skew property.

atoms.idea: Choosing e_N large enough guarantees all tensions positive.
atoms.feynman: Wind them all a bit tighter and you're safe.
atoms.visual: e_N slider: the minimum stretch bar crosses zero → lime ✓.

atoms.idea: Extensions: mixed rigid/elastic networks and tendons spanning two links (exercises).
atoms.feynman: Mix rubber bands and fishing line, or tie strings between bones.
atoms.visual: Per-tendon toggle (rigid/elastic) and an option to anchor a string between two links.

atoms.idea: Section 6.5 heading: control of robot hands.
Goal: extend Chapter 4's controllers to grasping and coordinated tasks, and discuss organizing complex controllers inspired by biological motor control.
atoms.feynman: Teach the hand the tricks that one arm already knows, then organize them like a brain does.
atoms.visual: Left: single-arm computed-torque scene thumbnail; arrow into: hand + box with the same controller badge; a small tree icon hints at hierarchy.

atoms.idea: Subsection 6.5.1 heading: extending controllers.

Two sub-problems: (1) track an object/workspace trajectory, (2) hold a desired internal force. With rigid, known geometry they partly decouple: get torques for tracking, then add internal forces to keep contacts in friction cones.
atoms.feynman: Carry a tray to the table (where it goes) while gripping it hard enough not to drop it (how hard you squeeze) — two separate dials.
atoms.visual: Two dials: gold trajectory follower and purple squeeze; turning the squeeze dial never changes the box's path.

atoms.idea: Class of systems: M(q)ẍ + C ẋ + N = F = GJ⁻ᵀτ, q = (θ,x), GJ⁻ᵀ: Rⁿ → Rᵖ onto; null(G) = internal force directions; M > 0 and Ṁ − 2C skew (true for all systems in the chapter).
atoms.feynman: Whatever the team of robots, to the controller it looks like one ordinary robot arm.
atoms.visual: The hand+box collapses to a single "virtual arm" with a blue effective-inertia ellipse at the box; the two property badges (M>0, skew) shown lime.

atoms.idea: Tracking: make x follow x_d(t) asymptotically; treat F as a virtual input, always realizable by some τ because GJ⁻ᵀ is onto.
atoms.feynman: Decide the push the box needs; the fingers can always produce it somehow.
atoms.visual: A pink virtual wrench arrow F on the box chases the gold path; fingers' torques recomputed each frame to produce it.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Any open-chain tracking controller works for constrained systems because only M̃ > 0 and skew Ṁ − 2C are needed (computed torque shown). Torques: τ = JᵀG⁺F + Jᵀf_N (6.36); f_N is free for internal-force goals (friction cones for grasping, often 0 for lifting), but dynamics also add contact forces.

atoms.idea: With F realizable and Lemma 6.1 properties, any Chapter 4 open-chain tracking controller can be used for x_d(t).
atoms.feynman: If it walks like an arm and quacks like an arm, the arm's controllers work on it.
atoms.visual: Controller cards (PD+gravity, computed torque) from the single-arm scenes dragged onto the virtual-arm box; all converge (lime error traces).

atoms.idea: Computed torque: F = M(q)(ẍ_d − K_v ė − K_p e) + Cẋ + N, e = x − x_d. M depends on θ and x; for holonomic constraints θ could be eliminated (needs a nonlinear inverse), but convergence proofs only need M > 0 and skew Ṁ − 2C.
atoms.feynman: Cancel what the box-plus-hand naturally does, then add a spring and a damper that pull it onto the path.
atoms.visual: Box follows a gold figure-eight; coral error vector e shrinks; K_p, K_v sliders reshape the exponential decay curve of |e|.

atoms.label: Eq (6.36)
atoms.idea: Pick τ with GJ⁻ᵀτ = F; GJ⁻ᵀ is onto but not one-to-one, the slack being internal forces. General solution τ = JᵀG⁺F + Jᵀf_N, G⁺ = Gᵀ(GGᵀ)⁻¹, f_N ∈ null(G); f_N doesn't affect tracking.
atoms.feynman: One push for moving the box, plus any amount of squeeze that cancels itself.
atoms.visual: Torque bars split pink (JᵀG⁺F) + purple (Jᵀf_N); sweeping f_N changes the purple part and contact arrows but the box trajectory trace is unchanged.

atoms.idea: Use f_N for force goals: in grasping, keep the net contact force in the friction cone (essential, since the model assumes contact). For coordinated lifting the structure enforces constraints, so f_N = 0 is common.
atoms.feynman: Holding a wet bar of soap: squeeze enough. Carrying a bolted-on box: no need to squeeze.
atoms.visual: Grasp mode: purple squeeze slider must keep arrows inside teal cones; lifting mode: welded contacts, slider defaults to 0 with no alarm.

atoms.idea: Actual contact force ≠ G⁺F + f_N; that is only the actuator part. Dynamics add more (§6.2.2), so guaranteeing cone membership requires computing or measuring constraint forces.
atoms.feynman: Swing the soap fast and your grip changes even if you didn't mean to squeeze harder.
atoms.visual: Contact arrow = purple actuator part + blue dynamic part; with fast motion the blue part tips an arrow out of its cone (coral) though the purple part alone looked safe.

atoms.idea: Often a detailed internal-force analysis is unnecessary (continued).
atoms.feynman: Usually the extra wobble is small.
atoms.visual: Slow-motion slider: at low speeds the blue dynamic part is a sliver.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: If dynamic constraint forces are small vs desired squeeze, use τ = J_hᵀG⁺F + J_hᵀf_N,d. Measuring and feeding back force naively creates algebraic loops (f = α(f − f_d) unsolvable); feedforward plus integral fixes it, with windup/noise caveats. §5.2: composite dynamics can be generated automatically.

atoms.idea: Assuming dynamic constraint forces negligible, final law τ = J_hᵀG⁺F + J_hᵀf_N,d with F from the tracking controller and f_N,d the desired internal force.
atoms.feynman: Move-the-box push plus your chosen squeeze — done.
atoms.visual: Two dials (tracking gains, squeeze target) feed one torque panel; ▶ shows the box tracking and the contact arrows holding at the target squeeze.

atoms.idea: Feedback on measured internal force must be careful: rigid systems transmit force instantly, so loops can be algebraic and ill-posed. A pure-force "robot" with f = α(f − f_d) only works if f = f_d = 0.
atoms.feynman: Telling someone "push exactly as hard as you are pushing, minus what I want" — there's no consistent answer.
atoms.visual: Loop diagram with no delay: solving f = α(f − f_d) plotted as two lines that only cross at the origin; set f_d ≠ 0 and the crossing point vanishes (coral).

atoms.idea: Fix: f = f_d + α∫(f − f_d)dt — feedforward plus integral compensation; f = f_d is consistent, so the loop is well-posed. Beware noise and integrator windup.
atoms.feynman: Start by pushing what you want, then slowly correct based on how far off you've been.
atoms.visual: Same plot with an integrator box: force trace climbs smoothly to the gold f_d (lime); a windup toggle saturates the actuator and shows overshoot (coral).

atoms.idea: Subsection 6.5.2 heading: hierarchical control structures.
A hand = robots coupled to each other and an object by velocity constraints; deriving the composite dynamics is mechanical enough to automate with symbolic tools.
atoms.feynman: Snapping Lego bricks together is easy; a machine can do it from the instructions.
atoms.visual: Finger blocks and a payload block click together; the composite (M, C, N) badge is computed automatically on snap.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Controlling a hand is hard: many actuators, constraints, sensors, a 30+-dimensional state, kHz-ish rates; biology faces the same many-DOF problem. Proposed: primitives to build controllers hierarchically. A "robot" = dynamics (M, C, N) plus inputs (x_d, F_d) and outputs (x, F).

atoms.idea: Controllers are the hard part: ~10–20 actuators, 10–15 constraints, state dimension ≥ 30, loop rates around 500 Hz; computing torques for one monolithic model within ~2 ms is often infeasible.
atoms.feynman: Trying to think about every muscle at once while catching a ball — too slow.
atoms.visual: A single giant block with a timer: its compute bar overshoots the 2 ms deadline (coral) as DOF slider grows.

atoms.idea: Biomechanics noted the same: how does a brain control so many interacting DOFs (Bernstein's question)? Robots share this complexity.
atoms.feynman: Your brain doesn't separately plan each of your 600 muscles to wave hello.
atoms.visual: A human hand silhouette with dozens of orange muscle dots lighting at once; a question-mark pulse at the brain.

atoms.feynman: Build the big controller from small reusable pieces.
atoms.visual: The giant block shatters into a tower of small blocks, each meeting its own deadline (lime timers).

atoms.idea: Every mechanism is a generalized "robot": a dynamical system M(q)q̈ + Cq̇ + N = F, fully described by (M, C, N).
atoms.feynman: Every brick has the same shape of plug: a heaviness card.
atoms.visual: Block with a blue (M, C, N) badge.

atoms.idea: A robot also has inputs (desired position x_d, desired force F_d) and outputs (actual x, measured F); not all are used by every robot. Relations depend on the robot (continued).
atoms.feynman: Each brick has two holes to plug commands into and two lights that show what it's doing.
atoms.visual: Block ports: gold x_d and orange F_d inputs on top, teal x and F outputs on the side.

Operations map robots to new robots, defined recursively. Attach: fingers + payload + constraint h(θ, x) = 0 → new robot in payload variables via Lagrange–d'Alembert.

atoms.idea: Actuated open chain: F = F_d and M q̈ + Cq̇ + N = F; desired trajectory input ignored until a controller is attached.
atoms.feynman: A bare robot arm does exactly what its motors push — it doesn't know where it's supposed to go.
atoms.visual: Finger block: orange F_d drives motion; gold x_d port greyed until a controller cap is added.

atoms.idea: An inanimate object is also a robot: inputs ignored, outputs report position and (if sensed) forces; (M, C, N) model its dynamics.
atoms.feynman: A box is a robot with no motors.
atoms.visual: Payload block: both input ports sealed slate; outputs teal; blue (M, C, N) badge.

atoms.idea: Operations take robots and return a robot; the new one's inertial data and I/O are defined recursively, querying and commanding its children.
atoms.feynman: Two bricks snapped together are still a brick — it asks its parts when you ask it something.
atoms.visual: Composite block with a glass top showing children inside; queries pulse down into children and back.

atoms.idea: Paragraph heading: attaching robots.

Attach: given finger robots, a payload robot and a constraint h(θ, x) = 0 (θ all finger joints, x ∈ Rᵖ payload configuration), build a new robot reflecting the geometric coupling — useful far beyond grasping.
atoms.feynman: Clip fingers onto a box with a rule for how they touch; out comes a "box-that-can-move-itself".
atoms.visual: Attach clip with an h(θ, x) = 0 tag; dragging finger blocks onto the payload block makes the clip glow lime when the constraint is satisfied.

atoms.idea: The new robot's dynamics are written in payload variables using Lagrange–d'Alembert, from finger (block-diagonal) and payload parameters (continued).
atoms.feynman: Fold the fingers' heaviness into the box, just like before.
atoms.visual: Finger badges flow through the clip and merge into the payload badge.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Attach details: M̃ = M_p + GJ⁻ᵀM_fJ⁻¹Gᵀ etc. with J = ∂h/∂θ, G = −(∂h/∂x)ᵀ, evaluated by querying children; state read by solving h or by sensors; commands distributed through constraints. Attach also covers workspace coordinates and redundancy variables. Control: wraps a robot, new attributes set by the controller.

atoms.idea: Attached robot: M̃ = M_p + GJ⁻ᵀM_fJ⁻¹Gᵀ, C̃ = C_p + GJ⁻ᵀ(C_fJ⁻¹Gᵀ + M_f d/dt(J⁻¹Gᵀ)), Ñ = N_p + GJ⁻ᵀN_f, J = ∂h/∂θ, G = −(∂h/∂x)ᵀ (J invertible). Evaluate by querying each child's inertia now.
atoms.feynman: Ask each finger "how heavy are you right now?" and add up their answers at the box.
atoms.visual: On ▶, query pulses fly to each child; their blue ellipses fly back up through the clip and add into the composite ellipse.

atoms.idea: State of the composite: read children's states and solve h(θ, x) = 0 for the payload pose, or use direct payload sensing (e.g. a camera); net object force similarly from contact and external forces.
atoms.feynman: Work out where the box is from where the fingers are — or just look at it.
atoms.visual: Teal output x computed from finger joints via h; a camera icon toggle replaces it with a measured x.

atoms.idea: Commands to the composite are distributed via the constraints; if fingers are uncontrolled actuators, desired forces go to actuators and desired positions are ignored.
atoms.feynman: Tell the box to push; it tells each finger how hard to push.
atoms.visual: F_d enters the composite's orange port and splits into per-finger torques J ᵀG⁺F_d flowing down.

atoms.idea: Data flow of attach is in Fig 6.11; attach also models other §6.2.3 cases: switching to workspace coordinates or adding internal-motion variables for redundancy.
atoms.feynman: The same clip can mean "touch a box", "hold a tool" or "track your elbow".
atoms.visual: Clip has three skins: grasp, workspace (G = I), redundancy (adds v_N port).

atoms.idea: Paragraph heading: controlling robots.
Control operation: attach a controller to a robot, producing a new robot whose attributes the controller decides; usually same state as the plant; given x_d, it buffers and tracks it (Fig 6.12).
atoms.feynman: Put a little brain cap on a brick: now you can tell it where to go, not just how hard to push.
atoms.visual: A controller cap snaps on: the gold x_d port lights up; the block now follows a gold path fed in.

atoms.idea: The controlled robot's (M̃, C̃, Ñ) are set by the controller: a fully compensating controller sets them to zero (continued).
atoms.feynman: A perfect brain cap makes the brick feel weightless to whoever is above it.
atoms.visual: Compensation slider 0 → 1: the badge's blue ellipse shrinks to nothing (greyed).

pages.summary: Figures 6.11 (two fingers attached to a payload: commands go down via h and JᵀG⁺, state/forces come up via h and GJ⁻ᵀ) and 6.12 (controller wrapping a robot). Compensation spectrum: full (zero dynamics to upper levels), none (pass through), partial. Building hierarchies begins.

atoms.label: Fig 6.11
atoms.idea: Data flow for two fingers attached to a payload: desired x_d becomes desired joints via h(θ_d, x_d) = 0, desired F_d becomes τ_d = JᵀG⁺F_d; upward, state via h(θ, x) = 0 and force F = GJ⁻ᵀτ; output dynamics M̃, C̃, Ñ.
atoms.feynman: Orders flow down the chain of command, reports flow back up.
atoms.visual: Animated wiring: gold/orange pulses travel down from the composite to finger 1 and finger 2; teal pulses travel up through the h-box and GJ⁻ᵀ-box to outputs.

atoms.label: Fig 6.12
atoms.idea: Controlled robot: control law takes x_d, F_d and robot outputs, sends command F_c to the robot object, and exports new dynamics M̃, C̃, Ñ.
atoms.feynman: A brain cap reads what you want and what the brick is doing, then pushes the brick.
atoms.visual: Cap box with gold/orange inputs and a teal feedback wire from the robot; an orange F_c arrow into the robot.

atoms.idea: Full compensation doesn't make the robot static — upper levels can ignore its dynamics. No compensation passes dynamics upward unchanged; partial controllers partly decouple.
atoms.feynman: A good assistant hides the messy details from the boss; a lazy one passes everything up; most do some of each.
atoms.visual: Compensation slider at 0, ½, 1: upper-level badge shows full, half-faded, grey ellipse.

atoms.idea: Paragraph heading: building hierarchical controllers.
These operations enable complex hierarchical controllers (continued).
atoms.feynman: Now stack the bricks.
atoms.visual: Empty tower scaffold appears.

pages.summary: Fig 6.13: human finger control hierarchy (cortex ~100–200 ms, spinal reflexes ~30 ms). Since a controller takes and returns a robot, it can be inserted at any level, so controller structure mirrors system geometry. Example 6.6 biological motor control begins.

atoms.label: Fig 6.13
atoms.idea: Hierarchy for a human finger: sensory/motor cortex at top, cerebellum/brainstem/thalamus coordinating, a pincer-grip composite at the spinal level, spinal reflex loops for each finger's muscles and joints; brain loop ~100–200 ms, spinal ~30 ms.
atoms.feynman: Your knee-jerk reflex reacts before your brain even knows; your brain plans the big picture more slowly.
atoms.visual: Two columns: left the human hierarchy (cortex, cerebellum, spinal cord, finger muscles), right the robot block tower; matching levels connected; clock icons show slow loops at top and fast loops at bottom.

atoms.idea: Because control takes a robot and returns a robot, it can be inserted anywhere, making hierarchies that mirror the system's geometric structure.
atoms.feynman: Every brick, plain or capped, still fits every other brick.
atoms.visual: Drag a controller cap to any level of the tower; the tower still clicks together (lime).

atoms.label: Ex 6.6
atoms.idea: Example: the biological hierarchy — cortex for perception/commands, brainstem/cerebellum for coordination, two fingers combined into a grasping composite at the spinal level (continued).
atoms.feynman: Two fingers become one "pinch" tool before the brain even thinks about it.
atoms.visual: Two finger blocks snap into a "pincer" composite at the spinal level of the tower.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Example 6.6 (cont.): spinal reflex loops react faster than brain loops; Fig 6.13 read as robots built from define/control/attach. Example 6.7: a planar two-fingered hand (Fig 6.14) with PD finger loops mimicking muscle stiffness, then the fingers attached as one Cartesian unit.

atoms.label: Fig 6.14
atoms.idea: Figure: planar two-fingered hand, two 2-joint fingers (left, right) holding a box, with fingertip and box positions marked.
atoms.feynman: Two two-knuckle fingers pinching a block.
atoms.visual: Two 2-link fingers (orange joints) and a blue box; teal contacts; pink fingertip points x_l, x_r, box center x_b.

atoms.idea: Each finger's muscles and sensors form fast spinal reflex loops, quicker than loops through the brain; feedback controllers drawn as double boxes.
atoms.feynman: Touch something hot: your hand pulls back before you feel the pain.
atoms.visual: Disturbance poke on a finger: the bottom loop (fast clock) corrects within a short beat while the top loop's pulse is still traveling.

atoms.idea: Reading Fig 6.13 with the operations: define two finger robots, cap each with muscle stiffness/reflex control, attach into a hand, coordinate with brainstem/cerebellum, and treat the pair as a pincer at cortex level.
atoms.feynman: Build bottom-up: fingers, then reflexes, then a pinch, then a planner.
atoms.visual: Tower builds itself block by block in that order, each step clicking into place.

atoms.label: Ex 6.7
atoms.idea: Example: hierarchical control of the planar two-finger hand (Fig 6.15), using dynamics and constraints from earlier examples, structured like the biological one.
atoms.feynman: Copy the body's plan into a robot hand.
atoms.visual: Robot tower starts beside the biology tower, level for level.

atoms.idea: Lowest level: PD laws on each finger, acting like muscle co-contraction stiffness (and possibly reflexes). Next: attach the fingers into one unit with complex dynamics and Cartesian configuration.
atoms.feynman: Tense your finger muscles a bit so they're springy, then think of both fingers as one pinching tool.
atoms.visual: PD caps (springs) on each finger block; then the two fingers clip into a "Cartesian pair" block with fingertip-position outputs.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Fig 6.15 controller stack: PD per finger → finger kinematics with feedforward (computed torque without error correction) making fingers look like Cartesian force generators → attach to box (grasp constraint) → computed torque on box trajectory at the top.

atoms.label: Fig 6.15
atoms.idea: Stack from top: box trajectory → computed torque → grasping constraint with box → feedforward on finger kinematics → PD on left and right fingers.
atoms.feynman: A tower: top says where the box goes, middle turns that into fingertip pushes, bottom keeps each finger steady.
atoms.visual: Five-level tower: gold trajectory card, computed-torque cap, attach clip with box, feedforward cap over finger-kinematics block, two PD caps on finger blocks.

atoms.idea: Feedforward (computed torque, no error correction) at the finger-pair level simplifies its dynamics for higher levels: the fingers look like two Cartesian force generators.
atoms.feynman: Make each fingertip act like a simple push-anywhere tool so the boss doesn't care about knuckles.
atoms.visual: Finger-pair block's badge changes from a complex ellipse to two simple pink force arrows at the tips.

atoms.idea: The box enters only now: attach the force generators to it, giving a robot with the box's dynamics but actuated by the fingers.
atoms.feynman: Only after the fingers are tidy do we glue them to the box.
atoms.visual: Attach clip joins the force-generator block to the box block; resulting badge looks like the box's ellipse.

atoms.idea: Top level: computed torque on the box lets you command box motions without muscle-level details, playing the role of cerebellum/brainstem coordination and error correction.
atoms.feynman: The boss says "move the box there" and fixes mistakes; the workers handle the rest.
atoms.visual: Drag the gold box target; the box follows smoothly; coral error trace decays.

atoms.idea: Information flow to the top-level law when evaluating box state (continued).
atoms.feynman: How does the boss find out where the box is?
atoms.visual: A "query" button at the top of the tower.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Top-level state query cascades down (hand → finger pair → left/right joints) and back up through forward kinematics and G⁺ᵀ; force commands cascade similarly. Benefits: fast low-level PD, distributed nonlinear compensation, task-space design with linear error dynamics.

atoms.idea: Query sequence: hand asks finger-pair for x_f, ẋ_f; that asks left and right fingers for θ, θ̇; finger-pair computes x_f = f(θ_l, θ_r), ẋ_f = J θ̇; hand computes x_b = g(x_f), ẋ_b = G⁺ᵀẋ_f. Force commands flow the reverse way.
atoms.feynman: Boss asks manager, manager asks workers, workers answer, manager summarizes, boss gets the summary.
atoms.visual: Press "query": teal pulses go down level by level, then numbers come back up with each level's transform box (f, J, g, G⁺ᵀ) flashing as it's applied.

atoms.idea: Control-engineering pluses: simple low-level PD can run at high rates to reject fast disturbances; Cartesian feedforward spreads nonlinear compensation across levels (parallel processors); top-level computed torque gives task-space design and linear error dynamics.
atoms.feynman: Fast reflexes at the bottom, smart planning at the top, and the work shared out among helpers.
atoms.visual: Each level gets its own clock (fast at bottom, slow at top) and its own CPU chip icon; a coral disturbance spike is flattened by the bottom loop before the top notices.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Summary, items 1–3: constrained Lagrange equations with multipliers and the λ formula; Lagrange–d'Alembert projection (agrees with substitution only when integrable); hand dynamics in effective-manipulator form.

atoms.idea: Section 6.6 heading: summary.
Recap 1: with Pfaffian constraints A(q)q̇ = 0, d/dt ∂L/∂q̇ − ∂L/∂q + Aᵀλ − Υ = 0, with λ = (AM⁻¹Aᵀ)⁻¹[AM⁻¹(F − Cq̇ − N) + Ȧq̇].
atoms.feynman: Rules about speed become pushes (λ) whose size you can compute.
atoms.visual: Map station "Constraint Forces": pendulum thumbnail with its purple tension arrow pulsing.

atoms.idea: Recap 2: Lagrange–d'Alembert projects motion onto allowed directions; with q = (q₁, q₂) and q̇₂ written through q̇₁, you get reduced equations; when integrable, this matches substituting the constraint into L.
atoms.feynman: Only check physics along the allowed directions; shortcuts are OK only for place-type rules.
atoms.visual: Map stations "Project & Drop" and "Substitution Trap": rolling coin thumbnail plus the lime/coral twin skates.

atoms.idea: Recap 3: hand dynamics with grasp constraint J_hθ̇ = Gᵀẋ: M̃ẍ + C̃ẋ + Ñ = F with M̃ = M_o + GJ_h⁻ᵀM_fJ_h⁻¹Gᵀ, etc., F = GJ_h⁻ᵀτ.
atoms.feynman: A hand holding a box behaves like one arm moving the box.
atoms.visual: Map station "Hand as Arm": the box's inertia ellipse inflating as fingers attach.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Summary, items 3–6: same equations for other systems via J and G; redundant (augment with K_h) and nonmanipulable (restrict with H) cases; tendon extension functions and coupling matrix τ = P f, tendon force-closure; structural properties M̃ > 0, skew.

atoms.idea: The same equations cover many other systems by choosing G and J_h.
atoms.feynman: Change the glue rule, keep the recipe.
atoms.visual: Map station "Teamwork Robots": lifting team, welder and chalkboard thumbnails.

atoms.idea: Recap 4: redundant systems augment with K_h (null(J_h)) and internal velocities v_N; nonmanipulable systems restrict object velocities with H, J_hθ̇ = GᵀHw; both return to the standard form.
atoms.feynman: Too many joints: add a knob. Too few: remove a knob.
atoms.visual: Map stations "Spare Joints", "Stuck Directions", "SCARA Pinch": knobs being added (orange +) and removed (coral −).

atoms.idea: Recap 5: tendon kinematics via extension functions h_i; forces f give τ = P(θ)f with P = (∂h/∂θ)ᵀ; force-closure if every τ can be generated (with positive tensions).
atoms.feynman: Strings over pulleys: a table says how string pulls become joint twists.
atoms.visual: Map stations "Tendon Pulleys", "Springy Tendons", "Always Taut".

atoms.idea: Recap 6: correctly defined, M̃ is symmetric positive definite and dM̃/dt − 2C̃ is skew-symmetric (continued).
atoms.feynman: The combined system is never weightless and never makes free energy.
atoms.visual: Two lime property badges glowing over every station.

atoms.idea: Page number.

pages.summary: Summary item 6 (cont.): those properties let Chapter 4 controllers extend, τ = JᵀG⁺F + Jᵀf_N with f_N keeping contacts in friction cones. Bibliography: constrained/nonholonomic Lagrangian mechanics, hand dynamics and control, operational space, tendon kinematics sources.

atoms.idea: Recap 6 (cont.): these properties let open-chain controllers extend; hand law τ = JᵀG⁺F + Jᵀf_N with F from the controller and f_N chosen to keep contact forces in their friction cones.
atoms.feynman: Push to move the box, squeeze to keep hold.
atoms.visual: Map stations "Track & Squeeze" and "Robot Lego": pink and purple torque bars; block tower.

Sources: classical derivations of constrained (incl. nonholonomic) Lagrangian mechanics, the first/second-order split for nonholonomic systems, multifingered hand dynamics and control extensions, operational-space methods, and the tendon-network formulation (with compliance and internal loops).
